News.title: Notorious Israeli mob boss shot dead by assassin at point-blank range in broad daylight
News.content:
Notorious Israeli mob boss shot dead by assassin at point-blank range in broad daylight

The leader of an Israeli crime group called the 'Caucasian Mafia' was shot and killed by a gunman after stepping out of a petrol station with two associates - a manhunt was launched

View 5 Images Israeli crime boss Yanis Yushvaev was shot dead in public (Image: @PrzemekShura/X)

CCTV caught the moment a dangerous Israeli crime boss was shot in the back of his head and killed by an assassin.

‌



Yanis Yushvaev, the head of Israel's Caucasian Mafia, was killed after stepping out of a petrol station with two associates, on Sunday afternoon. Footage from the petrol station, in the town of Caesarea, between Tel Aviv and Haifa, showed the crime boss and two men walking out of the building while another man, wearing a grey hoodie and cap, walked up the stairs and stood to the side.

‌



The assassin, who made it seem like he was waiting to go into the petrol station, suddenly turned around after the three men walked past and pulled a gun out of his pocket.

‌



View 5 Images Israeli crime boss Yanis Yushvaev was shot dead in public (Image: @PrzemekShura/X)

This shocking footage then showed the killer point the gun right at the back of Yushvaev's head before he pulled the trigger. The 40-year-old mob boss collapsed to the ground and the assassin fled the scene.

One of the crime leader's accomplices attempted to run away as the other man stood and looked around in shock. Yushvaev sustained critical injuries and was pronounced dead shortly after.

‌



View 5 Images Yanis Yushvaev was arrested by police multiple times but never convicted of a crime (Image: @PrzemekShura/X)

Police have launched a probe into the shocking daylight killing and a manhunt for suspects, who they believe fled the scene in vehicles.

Yushvaev in the past claimed he was just a restaurant owning businessman who "drives a Bentley, and that bothers police", but cops said he was the head of "a criminal gang in blood feuds".

‌



View 5 Images The assassin killed the crime boss outside a petrol station (Image: @PrzemekShura/X)

The man had been arrested several times on suspicion of involvement in grenade attacks, shootings and car burnings. Despite this, none of the cases ended up in a conviction, according to the Times of Israel.

Yushvaev was last arrested at Ben Gurion Airport, in Tel Aviv, after travelling from Russia in February - he was released days later. An unnamed police officer previously told Israel's Channel 12 it was "hard to convict him".

Article continues below

View 5 Images The gunman pulled the weapon out of his pocket (Image: @PrzemekShura/X)

This cop said the mob boss "almost never talks on the phone" as he believed his devices were wiretapped and only allegedly only communicated through his "loyal" associates.

Yushvaev, in 2021, was charged and accused of threatening a businessman over an alleged $1.1m debt, according to Ynet. Prosecutors said that when the businessman told the mob boss he could not afford to pay that money within a month Yushvaev allegedly told the man to take out a loan or sell him house, adding: "You have until Dec. 1 to transfer $1.1 million to me or we'll eliminate you."

News.title: Back-to-school warning as working parents lose £843 caring for poorly children
News.content:
Back-to-school warning as working parents lose £843 caring for poorly children

Parents lose an average of £843 in earnings each academic year taking time off work to care for poorly kids - as nutrition expert reveals how to prepare ahead of the new term.

View 3 Images Tonic Health is highlighting the impact childhood illness has on working families (Image: PinPep)

Parents lose an average of £843 in wages throughout the school year while looking after their poorly children. Tummy bugs, colds, fevers and coughs are the most frequent ailments to have kept youngsters off school over the past year.

‌



Research involving 1,000 parents of children aged five to 12 revealed six in 10 (63%) have been forced to take time off work as a consequence – averaging half a week – leading to heightened stress (37%) and having to dip into annual leave (20%).

‌



For 32%, their child's illness had impacted a work opportunity, such as missing a deadline or declining a project, while some had been perceived as less dependable.

‌



A third (31%) have sent their kids back to school before they'd fully recovered, as they couldn't afford more time off work, or had crucial commitments they couldn't miss.

View 3 Images Parents lose an average of £843 in earnings each school year caring for sick children

The research was commissioned by Tonic Health, which produces Kids Gummies providing 14 essential vitamins, minerals and plant-based nutrients to support children's growth, cognitive development and immune systems.

‌



The company is working with its head of nutrition, Natalie Louise Burrows, to offer advice for parents wanting to support their children's immunity as the new school year looms.

She said: "A strong immune system starts with the basics. Nutritious meals, plenty of sleep and a steady routine in the run-up to school can help kids stay fit and ready for the term ahead.

"It's understandable that many parents worry about the bugs and viruses which can spread when children return to the classroom, particularly when illness can affect family life as well as school attendance.

‌



"While getting ill is a normal part of childhood, taking steps to support overall wellbeing ahead of a new term can help children feel ready for the year ahead."

View 3 Images A third of parents have had to send their children back to school before they've fully recovered (Image: PinPep)

The research revealed that 46% of parents have worked from home while looking after a poorly child, and 44% have depended on their partner taking time off work.

‌



Meanwhile, 47% of parents are dreading the return to school because of the bugs and viruses their child could bring back home - particularly as 30% believe their little ones are more susceptible to illness during term time than during the school holidays.

Of those whose child fell ill after starting school, 57% said it occurred within the first month of term, including 13% within the first week. In line with this, 53% are worried about the number of illnesses their child goes through each year.

Parents say it has become 'normal' for primary school-aged children to suffer four colds over a typical 12-month period. As a result, almost all (96%) agree that maintaining a strong immune system is vital in helping children have a successful school term.

Article continues below

Ahead of the new term, 61% spent the most time sorting out school uniforms, while 36% concentrated on new shoes and 32% on getting sleep routines back on track. Yet just 26% said that immune support or vitamins were amongst the things they devoted the most time to preparing ahead of the return to school.

News.title: Girl dies as air ambulance scrambled to Cornwall cricket club tragedy
News.content:
Girl dies as air ambulance scrambled to Cornwall cricket club tragedy

Emergency services were called to Grampound Road Cricket Club near St Austell as the girl was taken to Derriford Hospital via air ambulance

View Image The chair of the cricket club has offered his 'deepest sympathies' to the girl's family and friends (Image: GOOGLE MAPS)

A teenage girl has died after collapsing at a cricket club in Cornwall during a "tragic incident".

‌



Emergency services including an air ambulance were called to Grampound Road Cricket Club near St Austell after it was reported the girl had collapsed.

‌



She has since died after she was taken to Derriford Hospital in Plymouth following the incident on Thursday evening.

‌



In a statement, Grampound Cricket Club said: "It is with profound sadness that Grampound Road Cricket Club can confirm a tragic incident took place on Thursday evening. A teenage girl collapsed and was taken to hospital, but has now sadly died. This is believed to be a medical incident not connected to cricket."

The club chair Lewis Sanders added: "Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and everyone who knew and loved her at this unimaginably difficult time. We will respect the family’s privacy and ask others to do the same.

‌



"We would also like to thank all those who responded on Thursday evening, particularly those who provided immediate first aid and the emergency services including the Cornwall Air Ambulance."

Cornwall Live reports two double-crewed land ambulances, an air ambulance, an operations officer and a doctor were sent to the scene.

A spokesperson for the South Western Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust (SWASFT) said: "We were called at 20:02hrs on Thursday, August 20, to an incident near St Austell. We sent two double-crewed land ambulances, an air ambulance, an operations officer, and a doctor to the scene.

Article continues below

"We conveyed one patient by air ambulance to Derriford Hospital."

News.title: 5 more arrests after deadly wrong-way crash on A66 including over ‘threats to kill’
News.content:
5 more arrests after deadly wrong-way crash on A66 including over ‘threats to kill’

Cleveland Police yesterday said 12 people had been arrested for various alleged offences following the deadly crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough - now five more arrests have been announced

View Image The scene of the crash on the A66 (Image: Iain Buist/Newcastle Chronicle)

Five more people have been arrested following a crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough that killed two police officers.

Cleveland Police yesterday said a "wide-scale investigation into the criminality which took place prior to the fatal crash" had been launched, and had resulted in 12 arrests.

Five more people have now been arrested on suspicion of various offences, including a 23-year-old man on suspicion of threats to kill, and a 16-year-old boy on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

The three others arrested are an 18-year-old man on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, a 21-year-old man on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, and a 55-year-old man on suspicion of assisting an offender.

The collision took place in the early hours of Saturday and involved two officers and five other people who were all killed seconds after a police pursuit had been abandoned. The five people, aged between 17 and 23, were in a Volkswagen Passat that was being driven the wrong way on the A66.

The car collided with a police vehicle which was going the right way, killing PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37.

The five individuals in the Passat have been named as Jakub Matusiak, 23, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-old Michael Robert Cahill.

A 19-year-old man from Redcar, who was arrested yesterday, has now been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life. He appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court this morning.

A 26-year-old man, also from Redcar and arrested yesterday, has been charged with possession with intent to supply class A and B drugs and possession of criminal property. He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Teesside Crown Court on September 21.

A 24-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon has been released on conditional bail. A 30-year-old woman arrested yesterday on suspicion of assisting an offender and has been released on conditional bail.

A 35-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon has been released on conditional bail. A 21-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage has been released on conditional bail. He has been remanded on recall to prison.

A 20-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order remains in police custody. A 61-year-old woman arrested yesterday on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate has been released on conditional bail.

A 47-year-old woman arrested yesterday on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs has been released on conditional bail. An 18-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs has been released on unconditional bail.

A 39-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs has been released on conditional bail. A 39-year-old man arrested yesterday on suspicion of threats to kill has been released on conditional bail.

Four of the occupants of the Passat had previous police convictions. Cahill was the only one out of the five with no previous convictions.

In July, Saddington admitted assaulting a police officer and causing racially aggravated alarm or distress to a second PC. He also admitted possession of a controlled class C drug, and possession of a knife in a public place on May 31 last year, and three charges of assaulting a police officer on the same date. He also appeared in a previous video of a police chase.

Worthy had used threatening abusive language to cause harassment, alarm and distress in 2024. He also admitted failing to surrender to custody on May 14, 2025, and he pleaded guilty common assault of a police officer on April 27, 2025.

He admitted driving without a licence, using a vehicle without insurance, driving without reasonable consideration and driving while using a mobile phone in June this year. Matusiak admitted using a vehicle without insurance and driving without a licence on March 22 this year.

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox described the investigation as "fast moving and complex, with significant links to serious and organised criminal activity".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect. We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice.

"Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organised crime. Officers and staff across Cleveland have shown incredible resilience in continuing their work in the face of tragedy.

Article continues below

"Two of their colleagues lost their lives while serving the people of Cleveland and, while the impact will be felt by our people for a long time to come, they have continued to act with the upmost professionalism. I am also extremely grateful for the support we have received, and continue to receive, from the public of Cleveland and our wider police family."

News.title: Mum attacked by shark said its face was 'horrific' and she only survived by thinking of her daughter
News.content:
Mum attacked by shark said its face was 'horrific' and she only survived by thinking of her daughter

'She's not going to have a mum' - thought Leah Stewart about her daughter as she was being attacked by great white shark which she desperately fought off

View 4 Images Leah Stewart said thoughts of her daughter helped her survive shark attack (Image: Jam Press/GoFundMe)

A woman who lost part of her arm in a shark attack in Australia has said the thought of her 18-month-old daughter helped her to survive.

‌



In her first public remarks since the attack two months ago off the coast of Sydney Leah Stewart, 35, said: "All I was thinking of was August and I thought, 'She's not going to have a mum'.

‌



“I couldn't handle that. I did not want her to grow up without a mum." Stewart described the great white that mauled her as a "monster" and said: "Its face was horrific. I will never forget. It was holding on to my leg.. I just thought, 'I've got to fight it and do everything I can to be here'."

‌



View 4 Images Leah Stewart described the shark's face as 'horrific' (Image: GoFundMe)

Major update issued on boy injured in crocodile enclosure zoo horror READ MORE :

Stewart, a teacher, was in a coma for a fortnight after the attack and underwent operations including the amputation of much of her left arm.

She felt she had been given "a second chance at life", she said, and had spent the past two months healing and slowly returning to normal life. A GoFundMe campaign set up after the attack has raised £300,000 for her support.

‌



View 4 Images She was attacked by a great white shark (Image: Discovery Channel )

The attack has prompted New South Wales to introduce drone patrols to monitor sharks. If one is spotted, operators sound an alarm ordering swimmers to shore. After the attack the off-duty lifeguard who saved Leah revealed she thought she had felt a dolphin before being bitten.

Charlie Verco, 25, was paddle boarding about 100 metres from Leah, when the attack occurred at Coogee Beach on June 13th.

‌



Leah was swimming about 30 metres from shore when she was mauled by a great white shark, with Charlie paddling towards the shark before helping the mother out of the water.

View 4 Images Leah Stewart talks about surviving shark attack (Image: Facebook)

Speaking on the Straight Talk podcast Charlie said it was not clear immediately before the attack that a shark was in the water. He said: “I actually found out that she felt the shark before she saw it and said it felt like a wetsuit material and she thought it was a dolphin, looked around and saw that it was a shark and that was when she started screaming.”

Article continues below

Despite paddling towards danger he said he thought his large paddleboard “would probably frighten the shark and scare it off.”

But those thoughts changed when he saw the size of the great white. I was paddling over with that kind of intention, still pretty scared, still pretty hesitant,” he said.

“I eventually saw the shark come out of the water. I saw the dorsal fin, saw the back, saw the tail, and I saw the size of it… this thing's a pretty solid animal.”

News.title: Sir Billy Boston: The working-class rugby league hero who broke through racism, barriers and generations of defenders to become a British sporting legend
News.content:
There was always something almost unfair about the sight of Billy Boston with the ball tucked under one huge arm.

Defenders knew what was coming and still could not stop it: a swerve, a sidestep, a brutal hand-off. If they did manage to get a hand on the rugby league star, his legs would continue pumping, taking the winger, built more like a forward, towards the line. Yet the man who terrified opponents became famous away from the pitch for a smile, a laugh and a modesty so deep that he seemed almost embarrassed by his own legend.

With Sir Billy’s death today, it ended one of the great lives in British sport. Following his passing, Wigan, the club he dedicated his paid tribute. Owner Mike Danson said: “Billy Boston was everybody’s hero, including my mum’s. His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game. But Billy’s legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man. He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations.”

View 5 Images A proud Sir Billy Boston is knighted by King Charles at Buckingham Palace in 2025 for his extraordinary services to rugby league (Image: Photo by Aaron Chown - WPA Pool / Getty Images)

‌



Sir Billy Boston dies as tributes pour in for rugby legend and World Cup winner READ MORE :

Kevin Sinfield knighted in King's Birthday Honours along with Helen Mirren and Lionesses READ MORE :

Rugby league fans were equally saddened. "Central Park was an awesome place for an eight- year-old Wigan fan on his first visit to the famous old ground. But the most awesome sight was Billy Boston, scattering defenders as he rampaged down the right wing. Not just a hero - more like a superhero," said lifelong Wigan fan Mel Woodward, 75.

Welsh Rugby Union, which Boston grew up dreaming of playing for but was destined never to play for the national side amid accusations of racism, also paid tribute. “Sir Billy Boston, one of the best-loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport, has passed away peacefully at the age of 92. The most famous son of Tiger Bay, he died overnight in hospital in his adopted home for the past 74 years, Wigan. His death came only four days after the funeral of his wife, Lady Joan, to whom he had been married for 70 years.”

Boston was rugby league’s supreme crowd-puller of the post-war years, Wigan’s record try-scorer, a Great Britain World Cup winner and a black sporting pioneer who crossed barriers long before the country was ready to admit how firmly they had been built. He died just weeks after that of Lady Joan, his wife of 70 years, and just four days after her funeral, a cruel closing chapter to one of rugby league’s most enduring marriages.

Boston’s numbers remain almost absurd. He scored 571 tries in 564 first-class rugby league appearances, a career total bettered only by Warrington great Brian Bevan. For Wigan alone, he scored 478 tries, a club record that survived generations of stars.

‌



William John Boston was born on August 6, 1934, at No 7 Angelina Street in Butetown, Cardiff, the sixth of 11 children. His father, John, a merchant seaman from Sierra Leone, was just 5ft 4in. His mother, Nellie, came from Cardiff’s Irish community. Tiger Bay was one of Britain’s oldest multiracial neighbourhoods, rough in places, poor in many, but crowded with families from across the world.

A few doors away grew Joe Erskine, the future British and Empire heavyweight boxing champion. Boston chose rugby, progressing from South Church Street School to Cardiff Schools, Boys Clubs of Wales, Wales Youth and the multicultural Cardiff International Athletic Club.

His dream was the Arms Park. He played for Neath and Pontypridd, and in 1952 impressed for Cardiff and District against a Cardiff side containing Cliff Morgan. Yet the call from Cardiff’s senior side never came. Boston later believed the colour of his skin was the reason, a view reinforced by the experiences of other gifted black and mixed-race players from the same district who were also overlooked in that era.

View 5 Images Boston became a Wigan icon after joining the club as a teenager, going on to score a record 478 tries in cherry and white (Image: PA)

‌



There was another contradiction in Welsh rugby’s supposedly pure amateur world. Boston later admitted that Neath slipped him £5 a match under the table. But once he accepted money from rugby league, the then rules meant there could be no return to union.

National Service took him to the Royal Signals at Catterick, where his rugby became impossible for league scouts to ignore. He scored six tries against the Welsh Guards in the 1953 Army Cup final. Wigan moved first. On Friday, March 13, 1953, chairman Joe Taylor and vice-chairman Billy Gore arrived at the Boston family home. They offered £1,000, then £1,500. Nellie, trying to get rid of them, demanded £3,000. To her astonishment, they agreed.

The teenager did not celebrate. He knew what signing professional forms meant. Years later, he recalled crying after Wigan's moneymen left and thinking: “Oh my God, what have I done?” His dream of playing for Wales at the Arms Park had disappeared with a signature. It turned out to be one of the shrewdest deals in rugby league history.

His A-team debut against Barrow in October 1953 brought two tries. His first-team debut, again against Barrow, followed in November and brought another. Boston could beat a man with pace, footwork or strength, and as he matured, he became even harder to stop. The late academic Phil Melling captured the contradiction perfectly: Boston was “a showman but never a show off”.

‌



Within months, aged 19, he was selected for Great Britain’s 1954 tour of Australia and New Zealand, the first non-white player chosen for a Lions tour. He scored 36 tries in 18 tour appearances, including a then-record four in a match against New Zealand. His career unfolded against a background Britain sometimes preferred not to discuss. Boston was adored in Wigan, but affection did not erase racism elsewhere.

When Great Britain travelled in the apartheid era, his race made participation in South Africa impossible. The sport that gave him his chance could not entirely insulate him from the society around it. At Central Park, he became royalty years before any king put a sword near his shoulder. With centre Eric Ashton inside him, Boston formed one of the great partnerships in the code. In 1956-57, he scored 60 tries, and he twice equalled Wigan’s then-record of seven in a match.

Wembley supplied the grand stage. He appeared in six Challenge Cup finals and won three, in 1958, 1959 and 1965. The 1959 final against Hull was Boston in full: two tries in a 30-13 victory in front of nearly 80,000. A year later, he scored twice as Wigan beat Wakefield Trinity 27-3 in the Championship final, giving the club its first title in eight years.

Internationally, he made more than 30 appearances for Great Britain and was part of the side that won the 1960 Rugby League World Cup. The strange sadness was that one of the greatest Welsh rugby players ever never won the full Wales union cap he had dreamed of as a boy. He appeared for Wales rugby league only in an uncapped match against France B in 1955, later receiving a heritage cap and number.

‌



View 5 Images Immortalised at Wembley: Billy Boston stands alongside rugby league greats in bronze, a permanent tribute to a player who changed the game (Image: Paul Harding/PA Wire)

For all the glamour of packed grounds, his was still the old working-class game. Players trained twice a week and held down jobs. He once joked: “When I was playing rugby union, I could go and have a smoke for five minutes.” League gave him rather less time to disappear. He remained at Wigan for 15 seasons before finishing with Blackpool Borough and retiring in 1970. By then, Wigan had become far more than an employer. It was home.

He had met Joan, a Wigan girl, on a blind date. They married and raised five children, building a life which endured long after the roar of Central Park had faded. In later years, as Boston lived with vascular dementia, Joan became his principal support. After playing, he ran the Griffin Hotel pub near Central Park, where supporters could find one of their old heroes standing behind the bar. He remained woven into the town.

The honours came as much for the man as the player. He was appointed MBE in 1996 for services to the community in Wigan and given the freedom of the borough in 2000. He entered rugby league’s Hall of Fame and the Welsh Sports Hall of Fame. Then came the statues. Wembley placed him alongside Eric Ashton, Alex Murphy, Gus Risman and Martin Offiah. Wigan put a bronze Boston in Believe Square in 2016. Cardiff finally brought him home in 2023, placing him with fellow “codebreakers” Risman and Clive Sullivan in Cardiff Bay.

‌



That homecoming mattered. Looking at the Cardiff statue, he said: “I may have been a Wiganer for the past 70 years but it looks as if I’m home to stay now.” By then, he had publicly revealed his dementia. His memory of individual matches could fade, but friends recalled how the mention of Ashton, Wigan or the old days could still bring back the twinkle. In February, he received a standing ovation at the annual Lions reunion lunch.

But his greatest official recognition had arrived the previous summer. On June 10, 2025, King Charles knighted him at Buckingham Palace for services to rugby league, the first player in the sport’s 130-year history to receive a knighthood specifically for the game. Sir Keir Starmer, the then Prime Minister, said that it was a “historic wrong” that the sport had waited so long to award him a knighthood. By that stage, Boston was suffering from dementia.

View 5 Images King Charles honours one of Britain’s greatest sporting pioneers as Billy Boston receives the knighthood many felt was long overdue (Image: PA)

The moment felt bigger than one man. Rugby league had long believed its heroes were overlooked by an establishment more comfortable with rugby union. Boston’s knighthood recognised a sport rooted in pit towns, mills and working-class communities, as well as a boy from Tiger Bay who had been denied his first sporting dream.

News.title: Fears for King of Norway as Palace confirm his ‘health has deteriorated’
News.content:
Fears for King of Norway as Palace confirm his ‘health has deteriorated’

King Harald of Norway’s health has worsened in recent weeks, after he was rushed to hospital and shared he was on leave from his royal duties

View 4 Images King Harald of Norway is Europe's oldest reigning monarch (Image: Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Ima)

Norway’s King Harald has been hospitalised after a major health scare, with the Norwegian Palace confirming his ‘health has deteriorated’.

‌



The King, 89, who is Europe's oldest reigning monarch, was taken to the National Hospital in Oslo last week with a rare condition called haemolytic anaemia, which is when the immune system attacks red blood cells.

‌



As a result of the disorder, he was placed on sick leave from his royal duties, with his son and heir to the throne, Crown Prince Haakon, acting as regent. The Norwegian Royal Family issued an urgent statement on Sunday with an update on the monarch’s health.

‌



View 4 Images King Harald's health has deteriorated, the Norwegian Palace has confirmed (Image: Getty Images)

The statement read: "His Majesty the King's health deteriorated over the weekend. The King is receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood, and has responded to this treatment."

They added: "His condition is stable. His Majesty will remain at Oslo University Hospital (Rikshospitalet) and is on sick leave until further notice." Many members of the Norwegian Royal Family have been seen visiting the hospital.

‌



The Palace confirmed the King’s condition within the last few weeks, saying he had "been treated with cortisone for the blood disease haemolytic anaemia. This has led to fluid accumulation in the body that requires treatment in hospital."

The disorder typically results in fatigue and breathlessness. The sole cause of the condition is not always obvious, but it can be caused by infections, other autoimmune conditions or certain drugs.

View 4 Images The monarch has been battling a rare condition called haemolytic anaemia (Image: Getty Images)

‌



King Harald, who has been on the throne since 1991, has suffered a series of health issues in the past. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that the King would make a ‘permanent reduction’ to his public engagements ‘out of consideration for his age’.

That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. King Harald was also taken to hospital while on holiday in Tenerife in February after a health issue.

As a result of the King’s health, his wife, Queen Sonja, will now undertake a series of royal engagements, due to take place on September 1 and 2, on her own while her husband remains in hospital. Harald and Sonja are due to celebrate their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.

‌



King Harald is not the only member of the Norwegian Royal Family who has been battling major health conditions recently, as his daughter-in-law, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, is still recovering from a lung transplant.

View 4 Images Both King Harald and his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit have had difficult battles with their health (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The princess, who is married to Crown Prince Haakon, underwent a lung transplant in June as she continued to battle pulmonary fibrosis, which had worsened in recent months following her diagnosis with the disease in 2018.

In July, she announced she had been discharged from hospital following her major surgery, as she issued an emotional statement thanking healthcare workers for their support.

According to Are Holm, Head of the Department of Respiratory Medicine at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet, the 52-year-old royal’s condition is “as good as can be expected”, adding that her rehabilitation will be closely monitored over the coming months.

News.title: British soldier dies on holiday in Bali in 'every family’s worst nightmare'
News.content:
British soldier dies on holiday in Bali in 'every family’s worst nightmare'

British soldier Finlay John Perkins tragically died while on holiday with his friends and family in Bali - with a fundraiser launched to cover the cost of repatriating him to the UK

View 2 Images Finlay John Perkins sadly died earlier this month (Image: Jam Press)

A young British soldier has died while on holiday in Bali with his friends and family.

‌



Finlay John Perkins, known as Fin, passed away during a trip to the Indonesian island earlier this month. His devastated loved ones said the holiday should have been filled with laughter and treasured memories, but had instead become “every family’s worst nightmare”.

‌



Finlay’s cause of death has not been disclosed, although a fundraising appeal was launched to cover the significant cost of repatriating the soldier to the UK.

‌



Finlay, who is understood to have been from the Milton Keynes area, was remembered as a caring and selfless soldier who always put others first. More than £17,300 was raised towards a £20,000 target before donations were paused.

The appeal said: “It is with broken hearts that we share the sudden and tragic loss of Cfn Perkins, who passed away whilst on holiday with friends and family.

View 2 Images Finlay’s cause of death has not been disclosed (Image: Jam Press)

‌



Police probe as several motorists seen driving wrong way on M6 following crash READ MORE :

UK weather maps show 13 counties face heavy rain on Thursday with thunderstorms READ MORE :

“No one ever expects a trip filled with laughter, memories, and time spent with loved ones to end in such heartbreak. What should have been treasured moments together has instead become every family’s worst nightmare.”

Paying tribute to Finlay, the fundraiser added: “Cfn Perkins was more than a soldier, more than a colleague, and more than a friend.

“He was a son, a brother and a loyal friend to so many. He was the type of person who would put others before himself, offer a helping hand without hesitation, and bring a smile to those around him. His loss has left a void that can never truly be filled.”

‌



Finlay’s heartbroken family also announced his death in a Facebook post. They said: “We are incredibly devastated to share the news of the tragic loss of our son and little brother Fin.

“Fin was a character like no other, the most caring, selfless, determined and kind man who touched the hearts of many.

“There are no words for how much you’ll be missed, but your grandad and best friend, Aidan, have been reunited with an absolute legend. We will forever love you with all our hearts.”

‌



The Royal British Legion also paid tribute to Finlay and offered support to his family.

It said: “We’re very sorry to hear of the passing of Cfn Perkins, and send our deepest condolences to his family, comrades and loved ones. We’d also like to extend our practical support to his family – please do feel free to contact us to discuss what we can do to help.”

A funeral notice confirmed Finlay died on August 9.

Article continues below

Family and friends have been invited to escort him on foot from the old police station on Newport Pagnell High Street to St Peter and St Paul’s Church on September 10.

Donations in lieu of flowers can be made to the Jack the Lad charity.

News.title: Five more arrests in wrong-way crash investigation
News.content:
Five more people have been arrested in an investigation into a wrong-way crash on the A66 in Middlesbrough which killed seven people, including two police officers.

Cleveland Police said a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group. A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.

All five remain in custody.

Twelve arrests had already been made, bringing the total to 17.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

All seven were killed when a Volkswagen Passat, going the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank, hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction at 03:39 BST on Saturday.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

On Monday, the force said it received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning.

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area while the second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday over suspicion of a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

Two men have since been charged as part of the investigation.

News.title: Trump may hope an 'economic onslaught' will pressure Iran - its leaders are betting otherwise
News.content:
The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.

Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.

His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?

Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.

What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.

The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.

The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.

If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.

They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.

Washington has also left little room for diplomacy.

Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash that followed a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It has since reopened.

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Young people leaving care have death rate four times higher than national average
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Moment tornado tears through southern France
News.content:
A destructive tornado has torn through villages in southern France, injuring more than 40 people.

An eyewitness from the village of Verzeille recorded the tornado forming beneath a thunderstorm. Winds of more than 100km/h (62mph) ripped the roofs off homes in Pomas.

Local authorities say about 2,800 households were still without electricity on Monday evening, while several roads were blocked.

More on this story.

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home from hospital
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Kate Hudson to make How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days sequel, 23 years on
News.content:
The movie grossed nearly $180m worldwide at the box office at the time.

The yellow silk Carolina Herrera dress Hudson wore near the end of the film also became a much talked-about piece of modern cinema fashion.

The star's most recent film role was in 2025's Song Sung Blue, which earned her a second Oscar nomination, following her first nod for Almost Famous back in 2001.

McConaughey's films include Dallas Buyer's Club, which won him an Oscar in 2014, The Wedding Planner and Magic Mike. He also appeared in 2008 movie Fool's Gold alongside Hudson.

Representatives for Hudson and McConaughey have been contacted for comment.

The new film would be the latest in a trend for nostalgic sequels in Hollywood, following The Devil Wears Prada 2 - which came 20 years after the original and also featured a magazine employee called Andy (played by Anne Hathaway).

In 2024, McConaughey told People magazine about his first meeting with Hudson before filming How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days.

"Immediately, we were comfortable with each other, and we jacked with each other, and we busted each other's chops, and we laughed a lot," he recalled.

"There was a bit of rock and roll exchange, like, 'Oh, this could be some heavyweight fun.' And I think that's why I was cast, and that's why, for whatever extent, it worked."

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
News.content:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at Â£2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston has died aged 92.

Last year, he became the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood.

Born in Cardiff in 1934, Boston grew up playing union but - overlooked by his home club - came to the attention of rugby league scouts while on national service in the north of England, signing for Wigan in 1953 as a 19-year-old.

Despite having played just a handful of games in league, the young winger's talent was quickly evident and Boston was picked for the 1954 Great Britain side that went to Australia and New Zealand - becoming the first black British player to tour down under.

He reached the 100-try milestone in just 68 matches after his switch from union.

Boston's scoring ratio is extraordinary, claiming 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan and helping them win three Challenge Cups and the Championship.

News.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
News.content:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

News.title: Man guilty of killing student after fake Rolex row
News.content:
A student who stabbed his former friend through the heart in Leicester after they fell out over a fake Rolex watch has been found guilty of manslaughter.

Harper Dennis, 19, plunged a knife five times into the chest of Khaleed Oladipo, 20, near De Montfort University in Leicester on the evening of February 3 this year.

A jury at Leicester Crown Court found Dennis not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter, having an offensive weapon and failing to provide the pin to his phone after a two-week trial.

Dennis, of Bath Lane, Leicester, was told he would be sentenced later on Tuesday.

Prosecutor Jane Osborne KC told the jury Dennis killed Oladipo, who he made friends with through online gaming, because of a "perceived debt".

The trial heard their friendship soured after an unsuccessful attempt by Dennis to sell a fake Rolex given to him by Oladipo.

News.title: Man convicted after being caught on CCTV upskirting girl in shopping centre
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to filming beneath a young girl's skirt in a shopping centre before running off and later being tracked down on CCTV.

Alex Allegretto, 39, admitted the offence of operating a mobile phone beneath the clothing of another person for the purpose of obtaining sexual gratification.

Police were called to St David's 2 shopping centre on the morning of 7 July after a mother reported Allegretto, who was unknown to them, for upskirting her daughter.

He was caught on CCTV heading back to his car and was later arrested for voyeurism at his home in Maesteg, in Bridgend County Borough.

Allegretto was sentenced at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on 5 August.

The CCTV footage shows Allegretto sat on a bench before quickly walking up behind the victim and her mum in the busy shopping centre and putting his phone by her legs before running away.

Sgt Luis Antony, from South Wales Police, said the victim had continued to be impacted by the incident.

"She is worried about people walking behind her and is anxious when out and about," he added.

Antony said that "nobody should be subjected to this kind of offence".

"The footage clearly shows Alex Allegretto's intentions and what he did to this young girl while she was innocently out shopping with her mother," he added.

"We hope the outcome at court provides some comfort to her and allows her to rebuild her confidence."

The court heard that Allegretto must be registered with the police in accordance with the Sexual Offences Act 2003 , externalfor five years.

He must also do 140 hours of unpaid work, complete rehabilitation activity requirements and pay a financial penalty of Â£199.

News.title: New 10p coin enters circulation - will you spot one?
News.content:
Something new might appear in your change when you pay in cash from now on: a 10p coin featuring the portrait of King Charles and the world's largest grouse.

Sufficient demand for the coins mean newly-minted 10p pieces are entering circulation for the first time for about four years, this time with a new design.

The Royal Mint says shoppers and collectors should discover the coins, which were minted and dated in 2023 and 2026, across the country.

The reverse side of the coin depicts an image of the capercaillie which is found in a small part of Scotland and threatened with extinction.

The redesigned suite of coins to celebrate the King's love of the natural world were unveiled in October 2023 by The Royal Mint.

The tails side of every newly-minted coin from the 1p to the Â£2 now features the country's flora and fauna - from bees to an oak tree leaf.

Coins in circulation in the UK carrying the portrait of King Charles have so far been limited to the 5p, 50p and Â£1.

Old coins with the image of the late Queen Elizabeth II can still be used, so the new coins are only struck in response to demand.

That is why, with 1.4 billion 10p coins in circulation, there has been no need for the new 10p to be released until now by The Royal Mint.

Now. 600,000 of these coins, dated 2023, and 6.5 million dated 2026 have been released to banks and post offices nationwide.

However, King Charles III coins still only represent about 1% of the 24.1 billion coins in circulation across the UK, making any new ones highly sought after by seasoned numismatists and new coin collectors.

News.title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says former Russian minister
News.content:
A Russian former deputy foreign minister has said there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints for British-made cruise missile components.

Andrei Fedorov's comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby President Donald Trump on Ukraine's defence needs.

Burnham's trip, should it go ahead, would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister.

"Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.

The UK has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

Fedorov, a pro-Kremlin commentator who frequently appears on Russian television, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media".

Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said: "It could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine.

"They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources."

The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international trip. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.

Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years.

In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots.

"There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."

In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."

"These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting.

In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".

They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the shadow fleet".

In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

News.title: Former TV news anchor admits to stabbing her 80-year-old mother to death on Halloween
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A former news anchor has pleaded guilty to stabbing her mother to death on Halloween morning last year.

​Angelynn Mock, who once anchored KTVI Fox 2, was arrested the same day after killing her 80-year-old mom inside their home in Wichita, Kansas.

Anita Avers was found with multiple stab wounds at around 7.50 a.m. and pronounced dead less than an hour later in hospital, Wichita Police Department said at the time. She had sustained stab wounds to her face, neck, torso and arms.

open image in gallery ​Angelynn Mock has pleaded guilty to first-degree murder after stabbing her mother to death last Halloween ( Sedgwick County Jail )

Mock told police said she had gone into her mother’s room that morning and found Avers sharpening knives, according to probable cause affidavit obtained by KSN.

The older woman tried to attack her and chased her daughter round the house while “spewing venom out of her f***ing mouth,” Mock claimed.

“I had to kill her, she wasn’t going to stop,” Mock said, per the affidavit, claiming her mother was “jealous” of a job opportunity that had come up.

open image in gallery Mock previously worked at KTVI Fox 2 before moving into sales ( Fox 2 St Louis )

Later in a police interview room, Mock began talking to herself, the document said.

​“I’d kill that bi*** to have my mom back any day,” she said, per the affidavit. “I don’t even know who she is anymore. I know, I believe she’s the devil.”

​The former news anchor’s stepfather Barry Avers told police Mock had previously been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, before that was revised to schizoaffective disorder.

open image in gallery Mock was deemed incompetent to stand trial, but that motion was later reversed ( Sedgwick County Jail )

​According to the affidavit, the stepfather said he believed Mock had been on medication and was close with her mom. He also claimed she had been laid off from her job as a news anchor following an incident involving alcohol.

​In January, Mock was deemed incompetent to stand trial, according to Sedgwick County District Court documents reviewed by Oxygen.com. ​However, in late July, that motion was reversed.

Mock pleaded guilty to first-degree murder at an evidentiary hearing on Friday and is due to be sentenced on October 5, KSN TV reports.

open image in gallery Mock is due to be sentenced in October ( KSN TV )

​Mock was a full-time anchor on KTVI Fox 2 in St Louis from March 2011 until February 2015, according to her LinkedIn page, having previously worked in a number of reporting positions.

By May 2015, she began working in a sales role and continued to work in other business-related positions.​ On her profile, she says that she “transitioned into sales because of the many similarities the two roles encompass.”

Joe Root revealed he was “really hacked off” after his England teammate Brydon Carse was handcuffed on a night out in the latest drunken incident to embarrass the team.

Carse is being ​investigated over an incident in Derby on Saturday night, after videos circulating on social media showed the Durham bowler in handcuffs being ⁠led away from a club by ​police ⁠officers. He was later “de-arrested”, police said, after agreeing to leave the area.

Carse has been dropped from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan starting on Thursday at Lord’s. He was not ⁠on England duty at the time of the alleged incident, ​after ⁠being an unused member of ‌the squad for the first Test which England won comfortably at Headingley, but is one of 30 players centrally contracted by the ECB.

The investigation by the Cricket Regulator comes five days after England’s returning captain ‌Root spoke of the players being “really ‌good role models and human beings” after a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

“If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off, really disappointed,” Root said, speaking at Lord’s on Tuesday. “I’m really disappointed that after last week’s performance, we’re sat here and we’re talking about something nothing related to it at all.

”In terms of the incident itself, it’s obviously with the regulator. There’s not a lot I can say on it. It’s in their hands now. I’ve spoken to Brydon – when I first found out, my first concern was him as a person, as someone I’ve spent a lot of time with in this dressing room. You obviously develop personal relationships with players, and I don’t think I’m speaking out of turn by saying he’s very upset, he’s been very apologetic, and understands his actions. I’m sure when he gets his chance, he will say that himself.

“It’s not the isolated incident itself. It’s the fact that we continually keep making stupid mistakes away from the game, and it’s detracting from what we’re doing on the field.”

open image in gallery Brydon Carse is the latest England player to be caught up in controversy ( PA )

Controversy has followed England around in recent times with off-field ⁠issues during last winter’s tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 following an altercation with a bouncer in Wellington as well as drinking during a mid-Ashes trip to Noosa.

This summer Ben Stokes broke a team curfew along with Gus Atkinson, with the pair dropped from the second Test against New Zealand at ‌the Oval, after an incident in which a member of England security was punched.

Root said he still didn’t believe a curfew was necessary to curb late-night incidents, but said he has reiterated what is expected from England’s players on and off the field in no uncertain terms ahead of the second Test.

“Certain things should stay in the dressing room, it’s a sacred place, but don’t worry, they are very clear on how things should be moving forwards. We’ve had a very robust discussion about where we currently sit. There’s real clarity there.”

Asked whether England players are being targeted by members of the public on nights out, Root said: “If we don’t put ourselves in certain situations, it’s not something that we have to worry about. Clearly, the landscape is very different now, where that is more readily available for everyone, and not every picture tells the truth. But at the same time, it’s understanding what impact that that could have ... this is about us collectively looking after each other, looking after the dressing room, looking after our environment, and looking out for each other.”

Root himself was involved in an altercation during the 2013 Ashes series, when Australian batsman David Warner threw a punch at his England rival in a bar in Birmingham.

“I’m not sitting here asking people to be saints,” he added. “Everyone’s going to make mistakes. That [Warner confrontation] was a learning experience for me, and I think it’s important for all to understand where we current are.”

Root said he had spoken to former England captain Stokes, who was pictured in the background of the videos of his Durham teammate Carse in handcuffs. “I have spoken to Ben, mainly over concern for Carsy. Now my concern is around the team, what we can do with this team onwards.”

open image in gallery Joe Root said he has made clear what is expected of his England teammates ( PA )

Root insisted this was a moment to reset, ahead of the arrival of new head coach Stephen Fleming next month.

“I think that actually we have an opportunity moving forward. Clearly, we’re not portraying ourselves how we want to, and I think we’ve got an opportunity to build a culture that’s very strong, that’s something that we can be proud of, is player-driven. Of course that’s not going to happen overnight.

“We’ve already started having conversations as a team about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England. But we want to create something that we can be proud of, and people that follow us can be proud of. We want the supporters to look at us and not just revere what we do on the field, but off it as well. And I think over the next little while, as leader of this team, with Stephen and with the group of players themselves, it is about creating something that is just that.

“I might only be in this dressing room for a couple more years, maybe a bit longer than that. There’s a group of players there that are going to be around for the next 10 years and they can achieve something over that period of time. So I’ve made it very clear what is expected of them, how we want to conduct ourselves to start with, and over time we’ve got to live it and show people what I see on a day-to-day basis in the dressing room ... That’s going to take a bit of work and time.”
