He has not yet told them who, exactly, benefited from the system he says the president inherited — and until he does, that is the answer this newspaper, and Liberians who found his words this week persuasive, should keep asking for.

World.title: Weah Warns African Leaders at 66th Annual General Conference of the Nigerian Bar Association
World.content:
PORT HARCOURT, Nigeria — Former Liberian President George Manneh Weah has delivered a forceful warning against the erosion of democratic institutions in Africa, cautioning that leaders who come to power through elections can still become authoritarian if they undermine the judiciary, weaken legislatures and suppress institutional checks on executive power.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Weah made the remarks Sunday, August 23, while delivering the keynote address at the 66th Annual General Conference of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, under the theme “Beyond Limits.”

Addressing lawyers, judges, government officials and other dignitaries, the former Liberian leader argued that democracy does not begin and end with elections, stressing that strong institutions are essential to preserving democratic governance.

“Democracy does not survive on the strength of elections alone,” Weah said. “Elections are the doorway into democracy, not the house itself.”

He said independent courts, a principled legal profession and effective legislative oversight are among the institutions that sustain democratic systems after elections have ended.

‘A Tyrant With a Certificate of Return Is Still a Tyrant’

Weah delivered one of the strongest portions of his address when he warned that the threat to democracy does not come only from military coups or defeated candidates refusing to concede elections.

He said democratically elected leaders can gradually undermine the same institutions that brought them to power.

“The danger is not only that soldiers might seize power in the night, or that a defeated candidate might refuse to leave office,” he said.

“It is also that a leader who arrives in office through a free and fair election can, over time and often gradually, begin to govern like the very dictators the ballot was meant to guard against.”

According to Weah, such leaders may attempt to influence the judiciary, pressure legislatures and turn institutions designed to provide checks and balances into instruments of executive power.

“A tyrant with a certificate of return is still a tyrant,” he declared.

He warned that democracy must be tested continuously after elections by examining how political power treats courts, legislatures, journalists and ordinary citizens.

Weah Calls for Strong Institutions

Weah referenced a statement by outgoing NBA President Mazi Afam Osigwe that “democracy cannot survive on strong men. It survives on strong institutions.”

He said the principle should be displayed prominently in African parliaments and courtrooms.

“The rule of law is not an abstract phrase for law school lecture halls,” Weah said. “It is the practical guarantee that a citizen’s rights do not depend on who is in office or what favor they can secure.”

He argued that the rule of law must provide equal protection to ordinary citizens, including journalists, traders and students, regardless of their social or political status.

“When that guarantee weakens, everything else in a nation weakens with it: investment, security, public trust, and peace itself,” he said.

Warning Against Judicial Interference

The former Liberian president also cautioned against executive interference in the judiciary, citing what he described as examples across the region involving manipulation of judicial budgets, questionable appointments, pressure on judges and the creation of special courts for political purposes.

He also referenced the wave of military takeovers that has affected several African countries since 2020.

While condemning coups, Weah argued that governments operating under democratic labels must also guard against institutional erosion.

He called on the Nigerian Bar Association to remain vigilant in defending judicial independence and citizens’ rights.

“This is why I say to you: the Nigerian Bar Association is not merely a professional association negotiating welfare for its members,” he said.

“You are a standing sentinel of this Republic’s democracy.”

According to Weah, when the legal profession remains silent, courts become more vulnerable to political capture, while a united and principled Bar can deter executive interference.

Weah Revisits 2023 Concession

The former president also used the address to revisit his decision to concede Liberia’s 2023 presidential runoff election to current President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

Weah said he congratulated Boakai while the vote count was still underway after preliminary results indicated that his opponent was leading.

He said some people around him had advised waiting until the final results were formally certified before conceding.

“I chose to concede while the counting was still underway, because I have always believed, and still believe, that the will of the people must stand above the ambition of any one man in a democratic setting,” Weah said.

He argued that electoral disputes and the failure to respect democratic principles can have serious consequences for national peace and security.

Weah said the NBA’s recognition of his 2023 concession was particularly meaningful because it demonstrated the importance of placing national peace and the people’s will above personal political ambition.

“If a small nation like mine can insist on that standard for itself, then surely this continent…can insist on standards beyond the limits others have too often assumed for us,” he said.

From Monrovia’s Ghetto to the Presidency

Weah also drew heavily on his personal journey, linking his rise from the Gibraltar community in Monrovia to the broader theme of overcoming limitations.

The former football star recalled growing up largely under the care of his grandmother in circumstances where few people expected him to reach the highest levels of international football or become president of Liberia.

“I did not accept them—not out of arrogance, but because the limits placed on us by man are not the same as the limits placed on us by God,” he said.

Weah became the first and remains the only African male footballer to win the Ballon d’Or, following a celebrated international football career before entering politics.

He later became a senator and was elected president of Liberia in 2017, serving from 2018 to 2024.

Beyond ‘Brain Drain’

Turning to Africa’s development, Weah said the continent’s greatest limitations are not a lack of talent or intelligence, but inadequate infrastructure and insufficient political and institutional organization to harness African expertise.

He called for a shift in thinking about the African diaspora—from viewing migration primarily as “brain drain” to developing systems that encourage “brain circulation.”

Weah argued that African professionals living and working abroad can contribute significantly to national development if governments establish mechanisms that enable them to share their expertise without requiring them to abandon opportunities overseas permanently.

He cited African diaspora remittances as evidence of the enormous economic contribution already being made from abroad.

“Imagine that same energy formally invited into legal reform and judicial modernization, as a deliberate national strategy,” he said.

Five Values for Breaking Limits

Weah said Africa’s effort to overcome its challenges must be anchored in five values: discipline, hard work, respect, perseverance and spiritual strength.

He drew parallels between football and the legal profession, saying talent without discipline is insufficient for success.

In the legal profession, he said, intellectual brilliance must be matched by discipline, ethics and commitment to justice.

He similarly described hard work as essential to overcoming corruption, weak infrastructure and institutional inertia.

Respect, he said, must extend to the dignity of every human being, national constitutions and independent institutions.

Perseverance, he added, is necessary because individuals and nations will inevitably face setbacks.

“Perseverance is the internal voice that says, ‘I will rise again,’” Weah said.

He also stressed the importance of spiritual strength, arguing that leadership should be viewed as temporary stewardship rather than permanent ownership of power.

‘Africa Must Stand Up for Democracy’

In closing, Weah called on African lawyers and institutions to defend justice, equality, accountability and free elections.

He urged the Nigerian Bar and legal professionals across the continent to remain independent and protect the rights of people regardless of wealth, political influence or social status.

“The law must never be an instrument of chaos. It must never become a weapon of war,” he said.

“It must remain what it was always meant to be: an instrument of remedy, of peace, of unity, and of accountability.”

Weah concluded by calling on Africa to stand for the rule of law, fairness, impartiality, gender equality, human dignity, peace, democracy and free and fair elections.

“Africa must continue in peaceful coexistence, and we must all stand up for the rule of law,” he said.

The address comes as Weah remains active on the African and international stage following his presidency. He has also signaled his intention to seek the Liberian presidency again in 2029, setting the stage for his continued political relevance ahead of Liberia’s next presidential election.

World.title: Liberian Model Francis Dine Set to Chase Africa’s Next Supermodel Crown
World.content:
MONROVIA — From the classrooms of BlueCrest University to the international fashion spotlight in Nairobi, Liberia’s Francis A. Dine is preparing to take her runway ambitions to the continental stage after being selected to represent Liberia at Africa’s Next Supermodel this November in Kenya.

Dine, a student of BlueCrest University, was discovered and recommended for the competition by Liberian-American international fashion show producer and talent scout Junda Morris, who has built a reputation for identifying and mentoring emerging African talent.

Morris said Dine’s striking presence, discipline and runway potential made her stand out as a promising representative of Liberia.

“As a Liberian fashion producer and talent scout, I am proud to see Francis step onto this international stage,” Morris said. “She represents the beauty, confidence, resilience, and limitless potential of young Liberian women. Nairobi is about to experience Liberia’s next superstar.”

From Liberia to the Continental Runway

Dine’s selection provides another opportunity to showcase Liberia’s emerging fashion and creative talent beyond the country’s borders.

Her participation in Africa’s Next Supermodel, described by organizers as one of the continent’s leading model-search platforms, is expected to bring Liberia into greater focus within Africa’s competitive fashion industry.

For Dine, the Nairobi appearance will be more than a personal modeling opportunity. It will also place her in a position to represent Liberia’s style, creativity and growing generation of young talents seeking opportunities on the international stage.

A New Face for Liberian Fashion

Morris’s involvement highlights the increasingly important role of talent scouts and fashion producers in identifying African models and connecting them with opportunities outside their home countries.

According to the statement announcing Dine’s selection, Morris recognized her potential and recommended her for the continental platform after seeing qualities he believed could translate to an international runway.

Her selection comes as Liberia’s creative sector continues to seek greater international exposure, particularly in fashion, music, film and other youth-driven industries.

‘Representing Liberia With Purpose’

As she prepares for her trip to Kenya, Dine is expected to carry with her the support of Liberians at home and in the diaspora.

Her journey from university student to continental modeling contestant is being presented as a story of ambition, confidence and opportunity—and a reminder that Liberia’s fashion talent can compete beyond its borders when given the right platform.

With Nairobi as her next runway destination, Dine now has an opportunity to turn recognition at home into a much bigger continental breakthrough.

Francis A. Dine — representing Liberia with elegance, confidence and purpose.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai: Flag Day Must Move Us To Action
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has urged Liberians to turn national pride into daily responsibility, warning that the Lone Star demands unity, discipline, and service as the nation marked 179 years of its flag.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Speaking at the official program marking this year’s National Flag Day, President Boakai said the flag is more than a national symbol. The event was held at the Executive Pavilion on Ashmun and Broad Streets in Monrovia.

‘’It is beyond the cloth and the recognizable colors of our flag lies a powerful expression of our national identity, our national history, and the struggles and aspirations of our people,” President Boakai told a crowd of government officials, diplomats, students, and citizens.

From Independence to Identity

The President noted that this year’s Flag Day, which follows last month’s 179th Independence Anniversary under the theme: “Strengthening National Identity Through Liberian-Led Historical Leadership,” must give Liberians one national identity – a visible, enduring symbol.

“It reminds us of who we are, where we come from, and the Liberia we must continue to build.”

He recalled the role of the seven women led by Susanna Lewis who sewed the first flag in 1847.

“Our national flag derives from the courage and determination to give physical form to the aspirations of our people as a nation in the making,” he stated.

Say No to Drugs – A Warning To The Students

Directing part of his remarks to young people, President Boakai called on students to live by the Flag Pledge by rejecting vices that destroy the future such as drugs.

“Learn the words of the pledge, but more importantly, understand and live by them. Loyalty to Liberia means respecting your fellow citizens, obeying the laws of the Republic, rejecting violence, protecting our national symbols, working hard and preparing yourself to serve your country,” he urged.

“In particular, I urge you to say no to drugs. Drug trafficking and the use of our country as a transit and operational center pose a serious threat, especially to our young people. Do not let anyone steal your future. Stay focused, disciplined, and determined to become the citizens that Liberia needs.”

The President praised students who participated in the parade, noting: “I saw discipline. I saw precision. I saw confidence and patriotism in the eyes of our young people. I am very proud of them.” He congratulated schools recognized as Best Salute, Most Disciplined, and Best Dressed.

Lead by Example – A Message To Adult Liberians

President Boakai challenged adults and public officials to match their words with action.

“We cannot ask our children to love Liberia while we undermine its institutions. We cannot ask them to respect the law while we disregard it. We cannot demand patriotism while we place personal, ethnic, religious, or partisan interests above the national good,” he declared.

As the head policymaker of the country, the Liberian leader announced the reintroduction of civic education in primary schools and the launch of standardized civic textbooks nationwide as a step toward restoring knowledge of the Constitution, history, and citizenship.

Commemoration, Not Complacency

Calling for national unity and development, the President intoned that the flag demands action against division and corruption.

“Our flag calls on us to action. It demands that we reject division, hatred, corruption, violence, and every force that threatens our national fabric,” he said.

“It calls on us to build a Liberia where our roads connect our people, electricity reaches more communities, healthcare improves, education is transformed, opportunities expand, our young people are not subjected to drugs, and every citizen can take pride under the Lone Star,” the President asserted, emphasizing that the flag belongs to every Liberian.

“To the elder in the village and the leader in the city, to the farmer in Lofa, the fisherman on the coast of Maryland, the worker in Monrovia, and to every Liberian at home and abroad. It belongs to all of us.”

One People, One Destiny

President Boakai called on Liberians to honor the sacrifices of the past and build for the future.

“May our flag continue to fly proudly over land and sea, and across the world, where for nearly two centuries it has served as a beacon of hope… May it remind us always that we are one people, one nation, with one destiny,” he said.

“As we always say, in all that we do: let us think Liberian, love Liberia, and together build Liberia. God bless the Lone Star. God bless the Republic of Liberia.”

Meanwhile, Education Minister, Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, said the reintroduction of civil and the launch of its textbooks will help propel Liberian young learners into responsible leadership and love for nation.

The Minister extolled President Boakai for his stewardship of the country that continues to bring improvement in the educational sector of the country.

World.title: Liberia: Prosecution Witness Fails to Link Kemayah to Sale of Saudi-Donated Rice
World.content:
Witness Says Former Foreign Minister Halted Distribution After Media Reports, Formed Probe Committee That Found No Evidence Rice Was Sold on Liberian Market.

By Willie N. Tokpah

MONROVIA- Prosecution’s first witness in the controversial Saudi-donated rice trial has provided testimony that could become significant to the defense of former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, acknowledging that the former minister moved to halt the distribution of the humanitarian commodity after reports that it was being sold, but that an investigative committee he established found no evidence that the rice had been sold on the Liberian market.

The testimony, delivered before Criminal Court “C,” has introduced a critical distinction into a case involving allegations over the custody, transfer and distribution of 29,412 bags of rice donated by Saudi Arabia for disaster victims.

While the prosecution maintains that Kemayah and other former government officials unlawfully interfered with the rice and contributed to its subsequent diversion, investigator John Kumeh of the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, AREPT, did not testify that Kemayah personally sold the rice, removed it from a warehouse, received it for his personal benefit or participated in any sale.

Instead, Kumeh’s account placed Kemayah’s initial involvement at the point when reports emerged that the donated rice was allegedly appearing for sale on the Liberian market.

According to the witness, Kemayah responded by directing the National Disaster Management Agency, NDMA, to halt distribution and subsequently established an inter-ministerial committee to investigate the allegations.

The committee, according to Kumeh, included Robert Sammy, identified as a former special assistant to the Foreign Minister; former General Services Agency, GSA, Director Mary Broh; NDMA Director Henry O. William; and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf.

He noted that the committee reportedly held several meetings at the GSA compound and its investigation did not establish that the Saudi-donated rice had been sold on the Liberian market.

Kumeh’s testimony placed an important evidentiary gap at the center of the prosecution’s case against Kemayah, that the allegation that prompted his intervention was not established by the committee he caused to be formed.

Evidence Against Kemayah

The prosecution’s case is not that the former foreign minister personally sold the rice.

Rather, the evidence presented so far appears to focus on his institutional involvement in the decision-making process surrounding the commodity.

The prosecution additionally alleged that Kemayah interfered with NDMA’s statutory custody of the rice and that the subsequent transfer of the remaining stock from NDMA to the GSA was unauthorized.

Kumeh testified that, following the committee’s work, acting Foreign Minister Thelma Duncan-Sawyer instructed the GSA to remove the remaining rice from NDMA.

He said the GSA subsequently moved 13,895 bags from NDMA.

The witness further testified that the GSA already had 11,200 bags of Saudi-donated rice in its warehouse, a movement that brought approximately 25,095 bags into GSA custody.

During that transfer, according to the testimony, 41 bags could not be accounted for.

It is this chain of institutional decisions, rather than evidence of a direct sale by Kemayah, according to Kumeh, that appears to form an important part of the State’s case against the former minister.

A Question of Authority

The trial has also raised a fundamental legal question over the authority of the Foreign Ministry to intervene in the custody of disaster-relief commodities.

Kumeh testified that the 2016 legislation establishing the NDMA placed policymaking authority in a statutory board comprising representatives from several government institutions.

Those institutions included Internal Affairs, Health, Justice, Finance, Public Works, National Defense, Agriculture, Mines and Energy, the Environmental Protection Agency and the United Nations Country Team.

The Foreign Ministry, the witness testified, was not listed among the statutory members of the NDMA board.

The prosecution therefore argued that the Foreign Ministry lacked the authority to direct the movement of rice under NDMA’s control.

For the defense, however, the central issue may be whether Kemayah’s intervention constituted criminal interference or an administrative response to reports that humanitarian assistance was being diverted.

The distinction could prove significant, that a minister’s authority to investigate a reported problem is different from criminal participation in the subsequent misappropriation of the property being investigated.

Hence, it is now incumbent on the State to ultimately establish not merely that Kemayah became involved, but that his involvement satisfied the elements of the offenses charged against him.

Where the Rice Went

The testimony becomes more damaging to other defendants as the investigation moves beyond Kemayah’s initial intervention.

Kumeh testified that investigators encountered significant difficulties tracing portions of the rice after it came under GSA custody.

He maintained, that some quantities were allegedly distributed to institutions and individuals outside the stated purpose of assisting disaster victims.

The Group of 77 and the Monrovia Central Prison were among those mentioned during testimony. The prosecution also introduced allegations involving several officials who allegedly signed for substantial quantities of rice. Kumeh alleged that Augustine Kollie was to signed for 4,282 bags and reportedly claimed that the rice had been distributed to disaster-affected communities, but investigators later visited some of the communities identified in the distribution records and, according to the testimony, representatives there denied receiving the rice.

At the same time, Edward Konneh was similarly alleged to have signed for 5,095 bags. Kumeh explained that again, field investigators reportedly found discrepancies between the records and accounts from communities identified as beneficiaries.

Archievico Doe was accused of receiving 250 bags. The prosecution also alleged that 5,000 bags were pre-positioned at the NDMA regional warehouse in Gbarnga, although the regional coordinator reportedly denied receiving them.

Those allegations, if established through evidence and cross-examination, could point to serious failures in the accounting and distribution of humanitarian assistance.

However, they do not, by themselves, establish Kemayah’s personal involvement in those transactions.

That distinction could become increasingly important as the prosecution attempts to connect the former minister’s decisions to the alleged disappearance or diversion of rice after the committee investigation.

The Committee That Found No Market Sale

Perhaps the most consequential aspect of Kumeh’s testimony is what the investigative committee did not find. Kemayah reportedly became concerned after media reports suggested that Saudi-donated rice intended for disaster victims was being sold, he stopped the distribution and established a committee.

The committee met. But according to the prosecution’s own witness, the committee did not establish that the rice had been sold on the Liberian market.

Kumeh testimony does not necessarily exonerate Kemayah from the charges against him, nor does it resolve what happened to the rice afterward, but creates an evidentiary distinction that the defense is likely to emphasize, that the former minister’s intervention was triggered by an allegation that his own investigative mechanism subsequently failed to substantiate.

Meanwhile, the prosecution will now have to explain why the decision to halt distribution and investigate the allegation should be treated as criminal conduct, particularly where the evidence presented so far does not show that Kemayah personally profited from the rice.

From Investigation to Alleged Diversion

The prosecution’s case appears to be centered on what happened after the original distribution was halted.

The State alleged that the transfer from NDMA to GSA removed the commodity from the institution legally responsible for disaster management and placed it in circumstances where substantial quantities could no longer be adequately accounted for.

The defense, however, is likely to argue that the chronology matters. Kemayah did not, according to the testimony presented so far, initiate the controversy by taking rice for himself.

His involvement began after reports of alleged market sales,Hehe ordered the distribution halted. He then established a committee to investigate and that committee did not establish that the rice had been sold on the Liberian market.

The subsequent transfer was carried out through other officials and institutions.

The question for the court will therefore be whether the prosecution can bridge that gap and prove that Kemayah’s actions were not merely administrative decisions made in response to reported irregularities, but constituted criminal participation in the alleged offenses.

Legal and Evidentiary Test

The case now appears to be moving toward a broader examination of institutional responsibility. There is little dispute from the testimony that questions arose over the accounting and distribution of the Saudi-donated rice.

So far, the prosecution witness has described his intervention, his establishment of the committee and the subsequent transfer of rice from NDMA to GSA.

But the testimony presented to date has not linked Kemayah directly to the sale of the rice.

It has not placed him as a recipient of the commodity.

It has not shown that he personally removed rice from an NDMA warehous,e and it has not established that he personally benefited from the alleged diversion.

That does not end the prosecution’s case, but it places the burden squarely on the State to establish the connection between his administrative decisions and the criminal offenses charged.

A Trial Now Defined by the Missing Link

The Saudi rice case is increasingly becoming a test of the difference between administrative responsibility and criminal liability. The prosecution may establish that government institutions mishandled humanitarian commodities.

It may establish that quantities of rice were distributed without adequate documentation. It may establish that some beneficiaries identified in official records never received the rice. The court will now determine whether the evidence proves beyond the required legal standard that each defendant committed the offenses charged.

For Kemayah, the first prosecution witness has so far provided a narrative in which the former minister entered the controversy after reports of possible diversion, not one in which he is directly described as a seller or beneficiary of the rice.

Additionally, the witness testified that the committee established by Kemayah did not substantiate the very allegation that prompted the intervention.

That testimony is unlikely to end the prosecution’s case, and gives the defense an important evidentiary point to develop as additional witnesses appear and the State attempts to establish the full chain of custody and responsibility

For now, the prosecution’s first witness has established that the Saudi-donated rice was intended for disaster victims, that NDMA initially handled its distribution, that Kemayah halted the process after reports of alleged market sales, and that he established a committee to investigate those reports.

But the same witness testified that the committee did not establish that the rice had been sold on the Liberian market.

As the proceedings continue, the central issue for the court may therefore be less about whether problems occurred in the handling of the rice and more about who caused those problems, who had legal authority over the commodity at each stage, and whether the evidence establishes Kemayah’s personal criminal responsibility.

Criminal Court “C” is expected to resume the trial on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, when testimony is scheduled to continue.

Until the evidence is fully presented and tested through cross-examination, the allegations against Kemayah and the other defendants remain allegations. The ultimate determination of criminal responsibility rests with the court.

World.title: Liberia: Tensions Rise After Midnight Immigration Arrests In Kparblee Forest, Nimba County
World.content:
Kparblee Town Chief Pastor Jonathan Tei

Kparblee Town, District Six, Nimba County — Tension erupted in Kparblee Town, District Six, Nimba County after immigration officers allegedly entered nearby bushland late at night and arrested 18 members of the Burkinabe Community who were harvesting cocoa, Town Chief Pastor Jonathan Tei has said.

By Franklin Doloquee / Nimba County

Chief Tei told reporters that the immigration team normally notifies his office and explains their mission when operating in the area, but that did not happen during the operation last Thursday.

Residents said officers entered the forest after dark, rounded up 18 people and brought them back to town.

Several women, including pregnant women — and children fled deeper into the forest and have not returned, the chief said, leaving families fearful and anxious.

“I was not informed. They did not come to my office to tell me the reason for entering the bush,” Chief Tei stated, saying, “If they go on operations here, they should inform me. This time they didn’t, and the people are angry.”

A community outraged

Anger swept through the Burkinabe Community after the arrests. Neighbors described waking to the sound of officers moving through the trees and the sight of frightened villagers being led away in torchlight.

Some sent relatives into the forest to check on women and children, but those searchers reported that the women remained hidden out of fear of further arrests.

Residents also accused immigration officers of a pattern of extortion and intimidation.

They alleged that officers routinely demand money and confiscate cell phones, returning them only after payments reportedly around 4,500 Liberian Dollars or its equivalent in CFA.

Chief Tei claimed the alleged practices have persisted despite repeated local complaints.

“There are several immigration officers working in the area over the years, yet they have not registered or coordinated properly with my office,” he intimated.

“People want fairness. They want a change because of the officers’ behavior.”

Local talks, limited progress

Following the arrests, local leaders and immigration personnel held reconciliation talks.

Chief Tei asserted that both sides acknowledged errors. Immigration officers admitted it was wrong to conduct a night operation without notifying local authorities, while some community members regretted calling for punitive action before all facts were known.

Despite the meeting, frustration remains high. Residents have urged national authorities to replace the immigration team stationed in nearby Bali Town, citing a long record of grievances.

“Bali Town is a peaceful, hospitable community that expects respectful treatment from government officials,” Chief Tei intoned.

He added that limited government services and visible development in the area compounded tensions.

“We see little infrastructure or services from government. Only one private donor recently supplied chairs for community meetings,” the chief said, noting the community’s sense of neglect.

Official responses and disputed details

Attempts to reach officials at the Liberia Immigration Service for comment were unsuccessful up to press time.

Lofa County Border Patrol Commander Amos Smith, however, confirmed to reporters that he led the group involved in the operation and that 18 Burkinabe were arrested in the forest at night.

“We are officers; we don’t have a specific time to do our work, so that causes us to go to the forest at night,” Commander Smith said, adding that the men arrested were taken to the next town while the women and children remained in the forest.

He did not provide details about charges or the location where detainees were held.

Several Kparblee residents, who spoke with FrontPage Africa (FPA), accused immigration officers of routinely confiscating money and phones and returning them only after payment.

Some witnesses alleged that officers have used threats of force to collect cash and phones before releasing people to return to the forest.

One community member estimated that close to L$5 million Liberian dollars has been collected from Burkinabe residents over time through supposed resident permit and registration fees demanded by some immigration personnel.

Residents also claimed that during Thursday’s operation, large sums of money were taken from those arrested before they were released. These allegations have not been independently verified.

Human impact and community fear

The arrests left families unsure where relatives were held and frightened to gather crops in the forest at night. Cocoa farms, a vital source of livelihood for many households, lie scattered through the bush around Kparblee, where narrow footpaths thread between stands of mature trees.

Villagers say the arrests disrupt both economic activity and social life. People avoid the farms after dark, school attendance dips when parents fear travelling at night, and local markets shrink as traders worry about encounters with security personnel.

The chief disclosed that women who fled into the forest face particular hardship.

Pregnant women and small children exposed to rain and insects in dense undergrowth risk health problems if they stay displaced for long.

Church and community leaders have started organizing search parties and bringing limited supplies to those hiding, but travel is slow and dangerous at night.

Calls for accountability

Community leaders have called on the national government to investigate the conduct of the immigration team and to hold any officers accountable if wrongdoing is found.

They also want clearer coordination protocols between immigration units and local chiefs to prevent future surprise operations that inflame tensions.

“It is not enough to apologize after the fact,” Chief Tei uttered, stressing “We need a transparent investigation, better coordination and a change in the behavior of officers who operate here.”

Human-rights groups monitoring the case say prompt and independent inquiries will be essential to restore trust between communities and state security services.

Until authorities clarify the circumstances and address community concerns, residents of Kparblee and surrounding Burkinabe settlements say tensions will likely persist.

World.title: SADC members seek qualifications harmonisation
World.content:
The Zambia Qualifications Authority (ZAQA) has emphasised the importance of mutual recognition of qualifications across SADC member states in enabling professionals to work freely and contribute meaningfully to the socio-economic development of the region.

Board Chairperson, Victor Zulu, has observed that Zambia’s universities attract students from several SADC countries, noting that many, however face challenges as they are subjected to further examinations and assessments back in their countries, before recognition.

Professor Zulu has explained that such bottlenecks hinder regional integration and professional growth, adding that similar challenges affect graduates from other countries seeking employment elsewhere in SADC.

He has stressed that harmonising qualifications across the region is therefore essential to remove such obstacles and allow graduates to work freely.

The ZAQA Board Chairperson said this when he opened a 3-day SADC Qualifications Framework Technical Working Group workshop in Lusaka, being attended by representatives of Qualifications Authorities from member states.

“So we are here also to look at the guidelines that will make it easy for our qualifications and national occupational standards to be recognised in the region”, Professor Zulu stressed.

Speaking at the same meeting, Chairperson of the SADCQF TWG who is also Chief Director of South Africa’s Department of Higher Education and Training, Philip Tshabalala, echoed similar sentiments, affirming his country’s commitment to the cause.

He pledged South Africa’s strong support for the SADCQF, further assuring of South Africa’s the country’s readiness to collaborate both within the region and across the continent.

He highlighted that South Africa was well positioned to contribute to the framework’s advancement, noting that it had championed this agenda through its leadership of the G20 Education Working Group in 2025.

“We have got the Ministry or the Department of Basic Education colleagues here. We have got the colleagues also from the Ministry of Higher Education and Training and our very own South African Qualifications Authority. And so we really want to welcome the SADCQF”, he indicated.

And speaking earlier, ZAQA Director General, Mercy Ngoma, explained that participants would review the portfolio of SADCQF activities for 2026 and 2027, share developments from member states, and advance regional guidance on referencing.

She added that governance, funding, and capacity renovations would also be considered.

Ms Ngoma noted that ZAQA had deliberately extended invitations to the Examinations Council of Zambia, TEVETA, and the Higher Education Authority to ensure Zambia contributed an integrated national perspective.

World.title: Hikapulwe assures prompt FRA payments
World.content:
Kafue District Commissioner Maurice Hikapulwe has reaffirmed government’s commitment to ensuring that farmers delivering maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) are paid without delay.

Mr Hikapulwe said farmers who have so far delivered their maize to FRA satellite depots are receiving payments promptly.

“Government is committed to ensuring that our farmers are paid on time for the maize they are delivering to the Food Reserve Agency. Farmers should therefore continue taking their produce to the designated FRA buying centers,” he said.

He noted that timely payment is important in helping farmers meet their financial obligations and prepare for the next farming season.

Mr Hikapulwe encouraged farmers in the district to take advantage of the FRA maize marketing season by delivering their produce to designated depots, and urged them to follow the required procedures to ensure the payment process runs smoothly.

He added that the government will continue monitoring the maize marketing exercise in the district to ensure the payment process remains smooth and timely.

“We want our farmers to benefit from their hard work, and that is why the government is making every effort to ensure that the payment process is smooth and timely. Farmers should have confidence in the process and continue delivering their maize,” he said.

World.title: Chongwe fire brigade retrieves body from dam
World.content:
Chongwe Fire Brigade on Sunday, 23 August 2026, retrieved a body of an unidentified man from Sunrise Dam in Silverest area.

Chongwe Municipal Council Assistant Public Relations Manager Cecilia Musonda said the fire brigade received a report of suspected drowning at around 15:59 hours, prompting officers to immediately attend to the incident.

Ms Musonda told the media that the deceased was an unidentified adult male believed to be aged between 35 and 37 years, discovered by members of the public who were fishing in the area.

She said upon arrival at the scene, fire brigade officers found the body floating near the water bank and immediately commenced recovery operations.

Ms Musonda explained that the officers successfully retrieved the body from the dam and handed it over to Zambia Police officers for further investigations and other necessary procedures.

She further said the body was later deposited to Chongwe District Hospital Mortuary, awaiting a postmortem examination to establish the cause of death, while police are expected to assist in establishing the identity of the deceased.

World.title: ZDA, LuSE Partner to enhance businesses
World.content:
The Lusaka Securities Exchange (LuSE) and the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at improving access to long-term capital for businesses and strengthening private sector-led economic growth.

Speaking during a joint press briefing today, ZDA Director General, Albert Halwampa, says lack of access to capital remains a major obstacle to the actualisation and expansion of investment projects in the country.

Mr Halwampa notes that the partnership will particularly support existing and expanding businesses, including small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to list on LuSE and raise capital for investment, job creation and economic growth.

He has disclosed that many investment projects facilitated by ZDA fail to reach financial closure because investors struggle to access appropriate capital.

Mr Halwampa has further noted that the partnership will also leverage the Zambia Investment Deal Room, a digital platform established to connect local and foreign fund seekers with potential fund providers.

He explained that the MoU will strengthen collaboration between ZDA and LuSE in investment promotion, access to markets, green financing and trade promotion, including support for exporters seeking capital to expand.

Mr Halwampa pointed out that SMEs are critical to the future of Zambia’s economy and should be encouraged to consider LuSE as an alternative platform for raising capital.

“ZDA has registered close to 3,000 greenfield and brownfield companies between 2021 and 2026, many of which require financing to actualise or expand their investments,” he added.

He further said the partnership will help create a pipeline of businesses that can access capital through LuSE while supporting the government’s agenda of promoting trade, investment, job creation and economic growth.

Mr Halwampa reaffirmed ZDAs commitment to work with LuSE to ensure that investors, both local and foreign, benefit from the opportunities created through the MOU.

Meanwhile, LuSE Chief Executive Officer Nicholas Kabaso said the partnership will connect ZDA’s investment promotion and enterprise development mandate with the exchange’s role of mobilising long-term capital.

Mr Kabaso also re-echoed that access to long-term capital remains a major constraint for businesses despite Zambia’s significant entrepreneurial potential.

He said the partnership will encourage more businesses, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), to consider the capital market as part of their growth strategy.

“Listing on the Exchange provides businesses with access to capital while strengthening corporate governance, credibility and visibility,” said Mr Kabaso.

He said the partnership will also focus on financial literacy, corporate governance, financial reporting and identifying barriers that discourage companies from accessing the capital market.

“LuSE currently has four companies with market capitalisation exceeding US$1billion, so there is need to develop a stronger pipeline of businesses capable of reaching that scale,” he added.

He said the success of the MoU should ultimately be measured by the businesses supported, capital mobilised, investments attracted and companies brought to the exchange.

Mr Kabaso said the partnership marks the beginning of efforts to build a pipeline from entrepreneurship to investment, growth and ultimately listing, further calling for continued collaboration.

World.title: Kateka: UPND’s Fear Of Petition Is Shocking
World.content:
Kateka, Katuta Demand Explanations As Courts Branded “Crime Scenes” During Petition Window

New Heritage Party president Chishala Kateka says the fear of a presidential election petition being exhibited by the United Party for National Development government is shocking, accusing authorities of deliberately obstructing a constitutional process by closing the very court premises where the petition was to be submitted.

In an interview, Kateka said government’s impunity and apparent fear of the petition had reached the point where the judiciary was instructed to close court premises altogether. She said the sequence of events, first soldiers stationed at the courts for several days, and now the courts themselves closed, meant the petition simply could not be submitted through ordinary channels.

“We are really shocked by the United Party for National Development government’s phobia of the presidential election petition,” Kateka said, describing petitioning as a constitutional right and questioning why authorities would move to close court premises if they had nothing to fear from the process. She said the government’s conduct in this instance amounted to abrogating the Constitution and proved that those in power do not respect the rule of law.

Kateka argued that allowing the petition to proceed would in fact be the best way to legitimise the election outcome, since courts provide the proper forum to prove a victory was legitimately won. She said the refusal to allow that process to unfold as normal suggested government itself was uncertain about what scrutiny might reveal, and that Zambians deserved to know what was happening to their constitutional rights.

Separately, losing independent presidential candidate Given Katuta has demanded government accountability for the classification of key public institutions, including multiple High Court buildings, as crime scenes. Her demand follows the designation of High Court premises in Lusaka, Ndola, Livingstone, Kitwe, Chipata, Kabwe and Kasama as crime scenes, a classification that forced them to shut their doors to the public nationwide.

Katuta said it was shocking that all High Court buildings across the country had been described in this way, questioning openly what sort of crime could plausibly have occurred simultaneously at so many separate institutions. In a statement, she noted that according to the yellow “crime scene” tape surrounding them, the High Court and the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security headquarters had now been declared crime scenes.

Katuta pointed to Zambia’s 35-year record of democratic governance since 1991, during which citizens had consistently held their leaders accountable for decisions affecting them, and questioned why that culture of accountability appeared to be shifting under the current administration. She said public institutions belong to the people of Zambia and demanded that government urgently inform the nation of what was actually taking place.

She further urged those in leadership to recognise that Zambians have the right to know what is happening in their country, particularly where a matter involves a public institution central to a live constitutional process. Both Kateka and Katuta’s interventions add third-party political voices, distinct from Mundubile’s own camp, to the mounting chorus of concern over the timing and justification of the court closures.

World.title: Observer Alleges Violence, Raids Marred August Election
World.content:
International Observer Alleges Violence, Raided Command Centre, Fatal Shooting Tied To Poll

An expert with an international election observers mission, Petteri Hakkanen, has produced a post-election analysis alleging that Zambia’s August 13 general election was marred by violence and irregularities, findings that reportedly prompted Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance leader Brian Mundubile to reject President Hakainde Hichilema’s declared victory and prepare a court challenge ahead of the constitutional deadline.

According to Hakkanen’s analysis, heavily armed plain-clothes men claiming to be police officers raided the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance’s media command centre in Ibex Hill, Lusaka, on the eve of polling day. Running mate Makebi Zulu said the men were searching for Parallel Voter Tabulation equipment and fired live ammunition at campaign staff during the raid. Alliance media director Brian Matambo confirmed that shots were fired during the incident.

Hakkanen pointedly noted that conducting a Parallel Vote Tabulation is not illegal under Zambian law, raising the question of what the government sought to prevent by targeting the equipment. He described the overall election as having taken place in a constrained democratic space, citing incumbency advantages and heavily biased state media coverage favouring the ruling party among his key concerns.

The analysis also flagged the timing of major electoral reforms, which Hakkanen said were adopted only three months before the polls, creating legal uncertainty in the run-up to voting. He further recorded intimidation of opposition figures and candidate withdrawals made under pressure during the campaign period.

Hakkanen said the Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended vote counting for about six hours on August 14 following reports of violence against polling staff and alleged theft of ballot papers. That suspension, he said, prevented observers from monitoring the counting process and caused significant uncertainty and anxiety among stakeholders. He noted that verification of electronically entered figures against paper tally sheets dropped sharply, from 100 percent to 81 percent, after counting resumed.

The most serious allegation in the analysis concerns events on the same day counting was suspended. Hakkanen said security forces raided a property linked to Mundubile in Kabulonga, Lusaka, an operation the government said targeted a suspected militia and led to the arrest of 11 opposition-linked individuals after weapons were reportedly recovered. That operation, according to Hakkanen, resulted in the fatal shooting of former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, whose death was only publicly announced six days later, following sustained public pressure.

Hakkanen said authorities initially gave conflicting accounts of events before ultimately confirming Kafwaya’s death. Amnesty International has since called for a prompt, thorough and independent investigation into the circumstances. Those subsequently charged with treason-related offences connected to the incident include Bishop Trevor Mwamba and George Chisanga. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has separately urged authorities to stop arresting people arbitrarily and to fully uphold the due process rights of all those detained.

The allegations contained in Hakkanen’s analysis sit in tension with an independent parallel vote tabulation conducted by a coalition of Zambian civil society organisations, which broadly affirmed the overall presidential result while noting a roughly three-percentage-point gap from the official figures. Whether Hakkanen’s more serious allegations of violence and procedural irregularity gain further traction may depend heavily on the outcome of the constitutional petition process and any independent investigation into Kafwaya’s death.

World.title: Zesco Girls ready for COSAFA Semis – Mwila
World.content:
Zesco Ndola Girls coach Florence Mwila says her side is ready to face any opponent in the semi-finals of the CAF Women’s Champions League | COSAFA Qualifier Botswana 2026.

The Ndola-based Zambian champions booked their semi-final spot in style, securing top spot in Group A with a 2-0 victory over hosts Gaborone United at the Gaborone United Stadium on Monday evening.

Zesco finished Group A with maximum 9 points from 3 games: following victories over Lesotho Defence Force (1-0) and Zimbabwe’s Herentals Queens (5-2).

After the win over the hosts, Mwila praised her team’s response.

“It is sweet three points. We are here to play the game. We knew we were facing a tough opponent, so we needed to improve in relation to the approach,” Mwila said.

The Ndola Girls are likely to face either Silver Strikers of Malawi or Mozambique’s Costa do Sol from Group B in the last four.

But Mwila insists there are no favourites.

“There are no preferences, we play any team that come our way. We are prepared. This is a tournament so you meet any opponent and you must be prepared,” she told journalists in Gaborone.

Group B concludes action on Tuesday evening.

Mamelodi Sundowns leads with 6 points, followed by Silver Strikers and Costa do Sol on 3 points each. Nsingizini Hotspurs of Eswatini are bottom with no points.

Zesco were runners-up last year after losing to Gaborone United in the final of the regional champions league.

This year, they have already beaten GU in the group stage and will be hoping to go one step further and qualify for the CAF Women’s Champions League finals.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 25, 2026
World.content:
Two UN Peacekeepers Killed in South Sudan Ambush

Two UN peacekeepers have been killed and seven others injured after unidentified gunmen ambushed a UNMISS patrol in South Sudan's eastern Jonglei state. The injured include three peacekeepers, two national police officers and two civilian staff. UNMISS chief Anita Kiki Gbeho condemned the attack and called for a prompt investigation, warning that attacks on peacekeepers may constitute war crimes. The incident comes as renewed violence puts South Sudan's fragile peace process under increasing strain. The country remains one of the world's most dangerous places for aid workers, with at least 36 humanitarian workers killed since January.

Prince Harry Steps Down from African Parks Board

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Prince Harry has stepped down from the board of African Parks, an African wildlife charity he supported for 10 years. However, he remains a supporter of its conservation mission. His departure follows an independent investigation into allegations that rangers managed and funded by the organisation committed human rights abuses, including beatings, rape and torture, against indigenous people in Congo-Brazzaville. African Parks admitted the abuses last year and said it had since strengthened its safeguarding measures and governance. Harry's exit comes as he and Meghan prepare to relocate with their children from California to the UK.

Kagame Slams 'One-Sided' US Sanctions Over DR Congo Conflict

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has criticised US sanctions imposed over Rwanda's alleged involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He said that they add to existing problems without addressing the root causes of the crisis. The US sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force and four senior commanders in March, accusing them of supporting AFC/M23. Kigali described the measures as one-sided. Kagame said international pressure should also address the role of the FDLR, the Congolese government and other actors, arguing that the conflict cannot be blamed solely on Rwanda. He said Rwanda would continue pursuing peace while taking measures it considers necessary to protect its security.

Former DP Gachagua Vows to Contest 2027 Presidential Election

Former Kenyan Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has said that his impeachment does not automatically prevent him from contesting the 2027 presidential election. Gachagua is challenging the decision in the Court of Appeal and potentially the Supreme Court. Gachagua argued that the High Court acknowledged his right to a fair hearing was violated. However, they still upheld his removal from office, which he called a constitutional "absurdity". Gachagua insists he remains a presidential contender, declaring that he is not a "kingmaker" but a potential candidate himself. He said that his opposition to President William Ruto is driven by concerns over governance rather than personal bitterness.

Close 

Tanzania Commission Begins Probe Into Election Violence

The Presidential Commission of Inquiry into the Individuals Involved in Violence and Violations of the Law during and after the October 2025 General Election has officially begun preparations to investigate those responsible. Commission chairperson retired Court of Appeal Judge Shaban Ali Lila said it will collect evidence from the public and other stakeholders. He said the commission would receive oral testimony, examine documents, and visit locations identified as connected to the incidents under investigation. The commission, established by President Samia Suluhu Hassan, will assess the evidence in accordance with Tanzanian laws and regulations.

US Seeks Wider UN Arms Embargo on Sudan

The United States has proposed expanding the UN arms embargo on Darfur to cover all of Sudan, as the country's civil war enters its fourth year. US Envoy Massad Boulos told the UN Security Council that weapons and financial support from outside powers were fuelling the conflict and proposed including drones and related technology under the embargo, as well as increasing monitoring. Sudan has backed a technical extension of the existing embargo but warned against measures that could weaken its army. Russia has expressed concerns about expanding the sanctions. The war between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions, with Darfur among the areas worst affected by violence.

World.title: South Africa: Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case - South African News Briefs - August 25, 2026

KwaZulu-Natal Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case
