08/25/2026 August 25, 2026 Germans swap friends for screens in their free time

Germans are spending less of their free time socializing with friends and more on individually planned and digital activities, according to a new representative survey.

The Hamburg Foundation for Future Studies found that just 19% of 3,000 respondents said they regularly went out with friends, down from 37% when its first "Leisure Monitor" was conducted 40 years ago.

Meeting friends remains the most important social leisure activity, but its role has weakened significantly over time.

"Traditional sociability is losing reach, while social contacts are increasingly shifting toward individually planned and digital forms," said Ulrich Reinhardt, the foundation's scientific director.

He said everyday leisure was increasingly dominated by internet use, television, music and smartphones. Digital activities have grown sharply:

82% listen to music digitally at least weekly, up from 52% in 2016.

71% use social media weekly, up from 48%.

33% play video games weekly, up from 9%.

Artificial intelligence is now used at least once a week by 42% of respondents, rising to 62% among 18- to 24-year-olds.

Reinhardt said younger users were turning to AI not just for information, but also for advice, reassurance and, in some cases, as a substitute for friendship.

World.title: El Gobierno aprueba un anteproyecto para reformar las leyes de extranjería y de asilo
World.content:
Desde la izquierda, la ministra portavoz y titular de Migraciones, Elma Saiz; el ministro de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska; y el ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres, se dirigen este martes a la rueda de prensa tras el Consejo de Ministros.

El Gobierno ha aprobado este martes, en su primer Consejo de Ministros tras el parón estival, un anteproyecto para reformar las leyes de extranjería y de asilo. “El objetivo es adecuar la legislación española al pacto europeo sobre migración y asilo”, ha afirmado el ministro de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, en la rueda de prensa posterior a la reunión. Además, se ha declarado “por primera vez en la historia” la situación de “interés para la seguridad nacional en Ceuta”, según ha explicado la portavoz del Ejecutivo, Elma Saiz, y se ha formalizado la creación de un mando único que se encargará de gestionar la crisis que azota Ceuta desde la entrada masiva a nado de unos 80.000 migrantes los pasados 30 y 31 de julio.

Durante la rueda de prensa, el ministro de Interior ha insistido en que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) no informó de la posibilidad de una entrada masiva en Ceuta. Se ha pronunciado al respecto tras ser preguntado por las palabras de la ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, que este martes en el Congreso ha sostenido que el CNI sí comunicó al Gobierno la eventualidad. Marlaska ha mantenido lo que ha defendido desde el principio: “No había ningún informe que atisbara que el 30 de julio iba a suceder lo que finalmente aconteció”. “Tenemos unos excepcionales servicios de información y estoy convencido de que en este caso han actuado perfectamente”, ha añadido.

Sobre el anteproyecto que reformará las leyes de extranjería y asilo, Marlaska ha asegurado que esta medida permitirá incorporar la figura del triaje para los retornos, que es obligatorio para los Estados miembros. Y ha señalado que, “aunque el reglamento europeo fija un plazo de hasta siete días, en España seguirán siendo 72 horas prorrogables solo por decisión judicial para limitar al mínimo imprescindible el tiempo que el extranjero deba permanecer en las instalaciones policiales habilitadas para el triaje sobre el procedimiento fronterizo de retorno”.

Las decisiones adoptadas por el Consejo de Ministros facilitarán “la tramitación de los expedientes de solicitud de protección internacional”, ha asegurado Marlaska. “La futura ley distingue entre el procedimiento ordinario de examen y un procedimiento de examen acelerado que ha de estar resuelto en tres meses”, ha apuntado. Y ha subrayado que los solicitantes a quienes se rechace su petición recibirán una notificación para abandonar el país. Así, ha sostenido que estas modificaciones legales también permitirán “la necesaria gestión de nuestras fronteras para garantizar la seguridad en nuestro país”.

Lucha contra mensajes xenófobos y habilita más espacios en Ceuta

En este sentido, la reforma impulsada por el Ejecutivo incluye los preceptos del pacto europeo sobre migración “que impiden la entrada en territorio nacional de aquellas personas que llegan de manera irregular a nuestras fronteras”, ha incidido Marlaska. Al mismo tiempo, el ministro ha subrayado el “enfoque garantista” con respecto a los derechos humanos de los anteproyectos elaborados y ha asegurado que el Gobierno está trabajando con la Fiscalía de Sala de Delitos de Odio para actuar contra los “grupos de extrema derecha” con discursos racistas y xenófobos.

Por su parte, el ministro de Política Territorial, Víctor Ángel Torres, encargado de coordinar el mando único para la crisis de Ceuta, ha aprovechado su intervención para defender la gestión del Gobierno, que ha calificado de “acertada”, al tiempo que ha recordado que “decenas de miles de personas volvieron a Marruecos”. Torres, además, ha celebrado la decisión del Ejecutivo en esta nueva fase en la que se ha aprobado la creación del comité para tomar el control de la situación en la ciudad autónoma. Y ha informado de que este martes el Consejo de Ministros también ha aprobado un real decreto en el que “se habilitan distintos recursos y espacios”, tanto de titularidad del Ejecutivo central como del Gobierno de Ceuta.

Al hilo, el responsable del mando único ha manifestado que “la prioridad del Gobierno de España es la devolución”, pero ha avisado de que actuarán teniendo en cuenta la ley. Así, ha aprovechado para afear al líder del PP y de la oposición, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que reclame la devolución de menores. “Es una imprudencia, una temeridad y faltar a la verdad”, ha criticado. Y ha insistido en que la repatriación de niños y adolescentes conlleva un proceso que se debe hacer según fija la ley, al tiempo que ha recordado que la delegada del Gobierno en Ceuta fue condenada por las devoluciones que se realizaron en 2021.

Preguntada sobre si el Gobierno ha hecho alguna autocrítica en su gestión en Ceuta, la ministra portavoz y titular de Migraciones, Elma Saiz, ha asegurado que desde el Ejecutivo se ha actuado “con humildad”: “Dejándonos la piel, no hemos dejado de trabajar ni un solo momento”. Además, ha adelantado que el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, comparecerá para dar explicaciones sobre la gestión de la crisis, aunque no ha detallado la fecha.

Seguridad nacional

Previamente a la reunión del jefe del Ejecutivo y sus ministros, Sánchez había convocado esta mañana al Consejo de Seguridad Nacional como un primer paso requerido desde el punto de vista legal para la constitución del mando único. Posteriormente, el Consejo de Ministros ha declarado la crisis de Ceuta un asunto “de interés para la seguridad nacional”. La decisión se ha tomado casi un mes después del inicio de la crisis, algo que ha sido duramente criticado por la oposición. El presidente ceutí, del PP, pedía desde hacía semanas ceder el control y la gestión de la crisis al Ejecutivo central al verse desbordado por la situación.

La creación del mando único viene acompañada de la puesta en marcha de una serie de ayudas económicas que buscan revitalizar la ciudad autónoma, cuyos negocios se han visto afectados tras la llegada de los miles de migrantes. No obstante, el plan de recuperación ―que contempla unos 180 millones de euros, según detalló el lunes el vicepresidente primero y ministro de Economía, Carlos Cuerpo― no ha sido aún acordado este martes en el Consejo de Ministros, pero se espera que se haga en las próximas semanas.

World.title: Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena
World.content:
Declarados patrimonio de la Unesco desde 2011, estos establecimientos de la capital austriaca ofrecen en verano sus terrazas para cenar bajo las estrellas, desayunar a ritmo de jazz o cumplir con el ritual del café con tarta viendo pasar la vida

En 2011, la Unesco declaró la cultura de los cafés vieneses patrimonio cultural inmaterial de la humanidad. La descripción oficial decía: “Son lugares donde se consumen el tiempo y el espacio, pero en la cuenta solo aparece el café”. Ciertamente, por muy elevado que sea el precio de la factura, nunca llega a pagar la experiencia completa: el derecho a sentarse durante horas leyendo los periódicos, siempre presentes en los expositores de prensa de madera; el asiento de primera fila a la vida, a la gente y al modo de ser de una cultura; el ritual diario de la tarta y el café de media tarde; el poder escuchar la música de un piano o la orquesta que toca en vivo, el sol que se filtra por la ventana anunciando la primavera, la conversación espontánea con el de la mesa de al lado o la posibilidad de encontrar un amigo, un amor, un confidente.

En una ocasión leí un libro sobre testimonios de supervivientes de los campos de exterminio nazis. Uno de ellos, francés, desvelaba su secreto para evadirse de aquel infierno. Varias horas al día, en su imaginación, dejaba el campo y se trasladaba a la terraza de un café parisino para tomarse un pastis.

Los rituales tienen una función y sirven para anclarnos a una cultura, a un modo de vida, a las costumbres de una época que ya se fue. Los cafés de Viena conocen esta fórmula y la cumplen a rajatabla. El café llega en una pequeña bandeja de plata, siempre acompañado de un vaso de agua del grifo (que en la capital austriaca es excelente, ya que, según dicen, procede de manantiales en los Alpes de Baja Austria y Estiria) y con una cuchara boca abajo. El camarero, a quien uno deberá dirigirse como herr ober (señor jefe de sala), puede parecer poco cordial, pero no se trata de un mal servicio: es el wiener schmäh (humor vienés), una mezcla de ingenio mordaz y hosquedad teatral que forma parte del espectáculo.

Una de las tartas que se sirven en el Café Central de Viena. Mark Green ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Quien piense que los cafés de Viena son simples cafeterías está muy equivocado. Fueron las oficinas de pensadores como Stefan Zweig, los cuarteles generales de artistas como Gustav Klimt; las cocinas de revoluciones, con chefs como León Trotski (que vivió en Viena de 1907 a 1914); también el consuelo de los solitarios, que formaban parte del mundo el tiempo que duraba un café, y el domicilio declarado de excéntricos, como el poeta Peter Altenberg, que recibía correspondencia en el Café Central de Viena.

La terraza del Café Central. E.Westmacott ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Hay que conocer ciertos códigos para evitar la mirada perpleja del camarero. Aquí no hay que pedir un café, a secas. Aquí hay que especificar. Un wiener melange, el café vienés por excelencia, es un expreso con leche caliente y espuma por encima. Básicamente, un capuchino. El einspänner es un café solo fuerte o un expreso doble, servido en un vaso de cristal con una generosa montaña de nata montada (originalmente diseñado para que los cocheros pudieran beberlo sin derramarlo). El großer brauner es un expreso doble servido con leche o nata aparte, para que cada uno añada la cantidad a su gusto. Y, por último, el franziskaner es una melange que utiliza nata montada en lugar de espuma de leche, llamado así por su similitud con el color del hábito de los franciscanos.

En verano, a algunos de los cafés más emblemáticos de Viena se añade el encanto de sus terrazas. Estos son los que cuentan con las zonas exteriores más hermosas, pintorescas o escondidas de la capital austriaca.

Café Landtmann (Universitätsring, 4)

Al lado del Burgtheater, el teatro nacional de Austria, y delante del Ayuntamiento, este café fundado en 1873 por Franz Landtmann presume de ser el más elegante de la capital austriaca.

Bienvenidos al universo de los desayunos largos y las comidas cortas de negocios, ya que cuenta con un menú del día a un precio bastante asequible (sopa y segundo por 16,90 euros o plato principal por 15). La cocina, aunque con buenos ingredientes, es algo aburrida, pero eso se subsana con los maravillosos postres, entre los que destaca el brazo de gitano (actualmente, con otros nombres) relleno de chocolate negro.

Con un deslumbrante mobiliario y una exquisita atención al cliente, todavía continúa siendo un lugar de encuentro para las altas esferas políticas y económicas del país. Por aquí han pasado Peter Altenberg, Sigmund Freud, Gustav Mahler, Max Reinhardt, Marlene Dietrich, Romy Schneider, Burt Lancaster, Hillary Clinton o Paul McCartney. Su terraza, rodeada de una jardinera con flores, es de las más agradables en los meses de verano.

Un mundo de exclusividad, pero también de vida urbana; ya que en Viena no solo los ricos van a estos cafés, sino también los jubiladas de clase media, los estudiantes y cualquiera que quiera aprovechar el sol del intenso, pero corto, verano.

Café Schwarzenberg (Ringstraße Galerien. Kämtner Ring, 17)

El interior del Café Schwarzenberg. Art Kowalsky ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Como la mayoría de los cafés de la Ringstraße, dispone de un schanigarten; es decir, una terraza. Término que no debe confundirse con el gastgärten, esa especie de jardín privado que tienen algunos bares, pero que no forma parte de la acera o la calle. Como todos los cafés vieneses, el Schwarzenberg es un viaje en el tiempo a una estética muy precisa, a un servicio impecable y una bandeja con vasos de agua y azucarillos, aunque la terraza se asome ya más al siglo XXI, de manera irremediable.

Además de eventos culturales (lecturas, exposiciones y veladas musicales), ofrece varios días a la semana música de piano y el jazz brunch, de 10.00 a 12.00. Durante la temporada de baile vienesa (entre noviembre y febrero), cuando la capital austriaca celebra más de 450 galas tradicionales —siendo su evento más emblemático el Baile de La Ópera—, este es uno de los pocos que ofrecen el llamado Katerfrühstück (literalmente, desayuno de resaca), en el que los asistentes al baile, al término de este (a eso de las cuatro de la madrugada), recuperan fuerzas con un pequeño goulash (un guiso de carne de ternera) y un seidl de cerveza.

Su selección de tartas es casi patrimonio cultural.

Café Museum (Operngasse, 7)

La terraza del Café Museum, en la capital austriaca. Emmanuele Contini ( NurPhoto / Getty Images)

Decorado por Adolf Loos, el establecimiento, que abrió sus puertas en 1899, pronto fue el cuartel general de artistas y escritores. Su decoración se distinguía de la de sus contemporáneos, más ornamentales, por su simplicidad y funcionalidad, que aún se observan en las sillas y mesas de la marca Thonet. A principios de los años treinta, el diseño fue cambiado considerablemente, pero la restauración de 2003 le devolvió su apariencia original. Se encuentra cerca del popular mercado callejero Naschmarkt, de la Karlsplatz y del Pabellón de la Secesión Vienesa, en la Ciudad Vieja de Viena.

A principios del siglo XX, cuando no existían las zonas VIP y los artistas se mezclaban con el pueblo llano, el café contaba entre sus habituales a Gustav Klimt, Elias Canetti, Peter Altenberg, Hermann Broch, Otto Wagner, Robert Musil o Joseph Roth. Y todavía guarda una estrecha y amistosa relación con la literatura, y hay lecturas mensuales seguidas de coloquios y firmas de libros con entrada gratuita.

La terraza del Museum recuerda a las parisinas, con dos filas de pequeñas mesas, donde en los meses de verano se puede degustar mil y una formas de desayunar, de tomar un menú del día o de honrar la vienesa tradición del café con tarta mientras se arregla el mundo.

Café Sacher (Philharmoniker Str., 4)

La terraza del icónico Café Sacher de Viena. Mark Green ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

La terraza de este café y hotel está revestida de un aura de exclusividad a pie de calle, donde es fácil acabar hablando con el vecino de mesa al mismo tiempo que se tiene la total certeza de estar en un lugar importante. Con su moqueta roja y su decoración de candelabros, cuadros de época y mesas de mármol, ha salido en películas como La dama de oro (2015) y Tarta Sacher (2022).

Esta especialidad dulce austriaca se puede degustar en cualquier café que se precie, pero quizás el nombre del lugar y el hecho de que aquí se sirve con crema batida sin azúcar, como manda la tradición, hace que mucha gente venga para pedir su café y su porción de tarta Sacher. Esta fue creada en 1832 por un joven de 16 años llamado Franz Sacher, que trabajaba en la cocina del príncipe Wenzel von Metternich como aprendiz. La historia cuenta que el príncipe había pedido a su jefe de cocina que preparara un postre para impresionar a unos invitados muy importantes, pero entonces el jefe cayó enfermo, dejando esta gran tarea al joven aprendiz, que creó un pastel de bizcocho con crema de albaricoque y chocolate.

Este café presume también por su impecable selección de los expresos más preciados del mercado cafetero y por su catálogo de tés, procedentes de todos los rincones del mundo. En temporada alta se recomienda reservar con suficiente antelación para vivir esta experiencia.

Café Rüdigerhof (Hamburgerstraße, 20)

Para desayunar, comer, cenar o para tomar el tradicional café con tarta, su terraza ajardinada, alejada de las zonas turísticas de Viena, es perfecta en los días de verano. Está además ubicada en un edificio estilo Secesión de 1902 y guarda una decoración interior estilo años cuarenta, con su tapicería, sus muebles y lámparas art déco, y sus visillos que tapan media ventana para ver sin ser vistos.

El edificio del Café Rüdigerhof. Zoonar GmbH / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Bajo sus árboles, los locales y turistas despistados hacen una parada para retomar fuerzas. Y si la Sacher es el bocado dulce que hay que probar en Viena, el salado es el schnitzel, una especie de filete empanado de cerdo, ternera o pollo, que el Café Rüdigerhof borda a las mil maravillas y sirve con ensalada. Los desayunos, a la sombra de los árboles o al sol dependiendo de la climatología, cuando los clientes son todavía escasos, son muy agradables, mientras que las cenas congregan a una mayor y más ruidosa clientela.

Café Prückel (Stubenring, 24)

El exterior del Café Prückel. Jon Bilous ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Este café, abierto en 1903 por Maxime Lurion, excampeón europeo de ciclismo, ha experimentado varias transformaciones en sus más de cien años de historia. Inicialmente conocido como Café Lurión, cambió su nombre a Café Miramonte antes de convertirse en el de hoy gracias a Wenzel Prückel, quien en 1906 logró obtener el permiso para colocar mesas en el exterior.

Destaca por su decoración de los años cincuenta, con especial atención a los detalles, incluyendo muebles de caoba con incrustaciones y sillas tapizadas en moquette francés. La ubicación es también privilegiada, ya que se encuentra entre Stubenring y Dr. Karl-Luegen-Platz. Además de su música de piano en vivo, bajo el café se encuentra el Lucky Punch Comedy Club, un lugar donde disfrutar de monólogos cómicos.

En el apartado de la gastronomía hay que destacar el café, que aquí es excelente, y el wiener melange. Otro punto fuerte es la prückel creme, una especialidad de la casa. Y, por supuesto, hay que probar el dulce por excelencia: el kaiserschmarrn, una especie de crêpe troceado y dulce que aquí es también todo un clásico.

World.title: Italia quiere poner orden en el caos de sus 12.000 playas privadas: más transparencia y nuevas tasas
World.content:
Entre el 33% y el 42% de los arenales del país son de pago. El Gobierno de Meloni, presionado por Bruselas, abrirá a concurso su gestión

Italia presume de sus 8.000 kilómetros de costa, pero disfrutar de ellos no siempre es gratis. Mientras que en otras partes ir a la playa significa buscar un hueco en la arena, en Italia la experiencia suele ser muy distinta. Encontrar un espacio donde plantar la sombrilla sin pagar puede convertirse en toda una aventura. En amplios tramos del litoral, el acceso al mar está gestionado por empresas privadas, mediante concesiones públicas, que han transformado las playas en un negocio multimillonario. El resultado es una de las estampas más características del verano italiano: bosques interminables de sombrillas perfectamente alineadas, acompañadas de sus respectivas tumbonas, esperando a ser alquiladas por precios que pueden superar los 35 euros al día.

Este modelo, muy arraigado en el país y marcado por una gestión plagada de irregularidades, afronta una reforma que lleva años aplazándose a pesar de la presión de Bruselas para poner orden. Las playas gestionadas por concesionarios privados no han dejado de ganar terreno. Según la asociación ecologista italiana Legambiente, ocupan ya más del 42% de los arenales del país. El Ministerio de Infraestructuras rebaja esa cifra al 33%, una diferencia que se explica por el criterio utilizado para el cálculo: el Gobierno utiliza para sus cuentas toda la línea costera italiana y no únicamente las zonas aptas para el baño.

Desde hace décadas, las empresas, casi siempre familiares —las concesiones suelen heredarse—, pagan cánones relativamente bajos al Estado por explotar espacios públicos, mientras los precios para los usuarios han aumentado de forma exponencial. Las concesionarias gestionan los servicios como los baños, las duchas, los vestuarios, los aparcamientos, además del alquiler de sombrillas y tumbonas. También controlan los chiringuitos y cafeterías y se encargan de las labores de salvamento. Mientras que las zonas públicas suelen estar descuidadas, a menudo sucias, y desprovistas de servicios públicos.

Se trata de un asunto sensible que divide a la opinión pública italiana. Para unos, las playas de pago garantizan orden, limpieza y comodidad; para otros, representan la privatización de un bien público que debería ser accesible para todos. La principal crítica al sistema es la enorme diferencia entre lo que pagan las concesionarias por explotar las playas y los beneficios que obtienen. El Estado recauda entre 80 y 100 millones de euros al año por las concesiones, mientras que el sector, marcado por la opacidad, mueve más de 2.000 millones de euros anuales, según distintas estimaciones. El propio Tribunal de Cuentas italiano ha advertido de que los cánones abonados por los empresarios no suelen ser proporcionales a los ingresos que obtienen.

Uno de los aspectos más controvertidos del modelo italiano es que las concesiones se han renovado durante años casi por inercia. Sin concursos abiertos ni una competencia efectiva y sin controles ni transparencia, los mismos operadores han conservado la explotación de amplios tramos del litoral público durante generaciones, consolidando un sistema difícil de encontrar en otros países europeos.

Un paso adelante

Bruselas lleva años reclamando cambios. La Comisión considera que Italia incumple la directiva Bolkestein de 2009, que obliga a garantizar la libre competencia en la adjudicación de este tipo de concesiones, y ha presionado repetidamente a Roma. Tras décadas de aplazamientos y enfrentamientos, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha abordado la cuestión. La reforma aprobada prevé que para el 30 de septiembre de 2027 salgan a concurso público todas las playas de pago, unas 12.000 repartidas por todo el país. Además, las concesiones tendrán una duración limitada, de entre cinco y 20 años, y habrá compensaciones económicas para los actuales titulares por las inversiones y obras que hayan realizado.

La perspectiva de abrir el mercado ha despertado, sin embargo, inquietud entre muchos empresarios del sector, que temen que los concursos favorezcan la entrada de grandes grupos turísticos o fondos de inversión capaces de desplazar a los negocios familiares que tradicionalmente han dominado las costas italianas.

World.title: Shrinkflation eases but manufacturers turn sneaky, watchdog says
World.content:
Shrinkflation is happening less often than a few years ago, but manufacturers are getting better at hiding it, consumer body the Consumentenbond has found in its latest sweep of Dutch supermarket shelves.

The organisation again found dozens of products whose contents had shrunk without a matching drop in price, and received fewer reports from shoppers than in previous years. But a hard core of producers are now shrinking packs so quietly that customers don’t notice.

The clearest example is Blue Band Vloeibaar, the liquid baking product, which dropped from 750 to 700 millilitres in March 2026 while the bottle and front label stayed exactly the same.

The new volume appears only in small print on the side, and the pack is still described as a “voordeelfles”, or value bottle. The recommended price held at €3.65, so shoppers pay more per millilitre either way.

Shrunk more than once

Some products have now been reduced two or three times over. Andrélon conditioner went from 300 to 250 and then to 200ml; on the last step the price rose from €5.49 to €6.49, a 48% increase per 100ml.

A bag of M&M’s, which held 440 grams in 2020, now contains 363 grams, leaving consumers paying about 10% more per 100 grams.

Manufacturers mostly blamed higher costs for packaging, raw materials, energy and transport. Mars, which makes M&M’s, pointed to recently changed rules it said might bar producers from sharing recommended prices – but, the watchdog said, as far as it could tell no such change had taken place.

Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar called on politicians to act. “When there is more in a pack, manufacturers shout it from the rooftops,” she said, “but when the contents shrink, they only adjust it quietly on the back.”

She wants producers required to state a reduction clearly on the pack, or supermarkets made to flag it at the shelf, as is already the law in France.

World.title: Fraudsters using iDeal switch to Wero to snare bank customers
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Fraudsters are sending out phishing mails to Dutch bank customers to try to take advantage of the switch from the iDeal payment system to Wero.

The fake messages typically tell customers they are due a refund as a result of the transition to Wero, the European-based system set up under efforts to make EU businesses less dependent on foreign digital services.

Victims are told to verify their identity by clicking on a link in the e-mail, which takes them to a page where the criminals can steal their login details.

The online fraud hotline Fraudehelpdesk.nl said it was currently receiving 100 queries a day about suspicious messages regarding iDeal, after a surge in activity in the last few months.

A frequently seen mail in recent days says the handover took place on August 24 and puts customers under pressure to claim their refund before the “deadline”.

Danial van Delft, CEO of Currence, the company that operates iDeal and Wero, told the Telegraaf: “This is a big change in the payments ecosystem and gives people with bad intentions space to abuse it.

“We see fraudsters becoming more and more inventive. They are trying to latch on to every hook and news item.”

iDeal said people should ignore suspicious emails and not click on links. “iDeal will never ask you to confirm personal details by email, start a verification process or install software,” the company said.

World.title: Villagers at centre of asylum row urge council to heal divide
World.content:
Residents of a Noord-Brabant village at the centre of a bitter row about plans to accommodate 50 asylum seekers have accused the local council of making the problem worse through its poor communications strategy.

Violent protests were staged in Engelen, on the edge of ’s-Hertogenbosch, after the council announced in April it would be housing a group of teenage boys and girls, all under 18, in a former police station on Beverspijken.

Opponents have staged marches to express their concern about women’s safety, while supporters say they have been subjected to a hate campaign, with swastikas and obscene words spray-painted on their homes.

At a council meeting on Monday night, residents on both sides of the divide appealed to the local mayor, Jack Mikkers, to talk to villagers before the final decision is made next month.

Around 100 people packed into the council chamber in Den Bosch and a side room set up as an overspill location for those who were unable to get into the public gallery.

The council says it has an obligation to accommodate asylum seekers under the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all local authorities to take in a fair share in order to ease overcrowding at the reception centre in Ter Apel, Groningen.

“Spend an evening walking through Engelen, ring people’s doorbells and listen,” said Tamara Govers, who organised one of the marches in May. “Come as a person, not an official, without cameras or press releases.”

Blacklist

Astrid van den Broek, who spoke in support of the plan, called for councillors to stop the threats and intimidation. “My name’s been put on a blacklist,” she said, adding that a man who threatened her when she filmed a group putting up protest signs was at the meeting.

“I’ve told security,” she said. “Don’t talk to me about being concerned about our women’s safety if the shelter goes ahead.”

Other villagers said the municipality had been too slow to respond to the menacing atmosphere in the village. “The shelter has driven a wedge between friendships,” said resident Eva Buijs.

Jack Burg, chair of local campaign group Veilig Engelen, said “better communication” from the council could have prevented the situation escalating.

Burg said the plans did not do enough to address concerns about the impact of the refugee centre on quality of life in the village.

“Conditions and rules have not been worked out,” he said. “We need more than this plan for a suitable accommodation facility. We want clarity, but that’s not what this is.”

Strict conditions

The council has set strict conditions for the centre, including a 10pm curfew and night-time security. Residents will have to move out as soon as they turn 18, most likely to smaller groups in Den Bosch.

The municipality also wants the refugee accommodation agency COA to send equal numbers of girls and boys, but that may be difficult to arrange because five out of six underage asylum seekers are male.

Some residents said they were not against accommodating refugees in the village, but called the empty police station on Beverspijken the “wrong location”.

One group produced data from decibel readings taken from the site that showed levels of 83 decibels had been recorded at night – 18db higher than the level permitted by the local environmental plan.

Others questioned whether the council and the COA could be relied on to stick to their agreeement to make the accommodation centre a temporary facility, pointing out that permits for other locations have been extended at the request of the agency.

World.title: Deadlock looms in budget talks as opposition drive hard bargain
World.content:
Talks to secure support from opposition parties for next year’s budget are entering their final days with no sign of a breakthrough.

Jesse Klaver, leader of the left-wing opposition group Pro (previously GroenLinks/PvdA) said the two sides had “not moved a step closer to each other” after emerging from negotiations on Monday.

Michiel Hoogeveen, of the right-wing JA21, accused the coalition parties of “kicking the can down the road”, while the hardline Protestant party SGP said a deal was “a long way off”.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has a deadline of August 28 to submit a draft budget to the Council of State before the formal presentation of his plans at the state opening of parliament on September 15.

MPs will not vote on the measures until late in the autumn, but the cabinet wants to do a deal with the opposition to secure majority support in both houses before budget day.

Yo-yo politics

Prime minister Rob Jetten said earlier: “This cabinet has big ambitions to make major investments in the next few years in more affordable houses, more security and the economy of the future. It’s good to do that with others if we want to avoid yo-yo politics.”

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of 10 opposition MPs in the lower house and 16 senators to pass its legislation.

Asylum minister and deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink, of the CDA, said the government was prepared to take “big steps” to accommodate the opposition groups. But Klaver said he had seen little sign of movement from the coalition.

Pro wants the cabinet to shelve plans to cut welfare spending by €6.5 billion in order to raise money for other departments, chiefly defence, where the Netherlands is striving to hit the new Nato target of 3.5% of GDP.

Wealth taxes

The party argues that the money should be raised by raising wealth taxes instead. “The cabinet seems to be mainly concerned with the position of millionaires in the Netherlands while we are worried about the people who are paying the bills,” Klaver said.

But Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, is opposed to wealth taxes and would prefer to make concessions to parties on the right such as JA21 and SGP, who want to see tax cuts instead. But SGP MP André Flach said on Tuesday that the coalition’s plans “are not enough at the moment”.

The SGP, which draws its vote from Bible-Belt communities, wants the cabinet to suspend plans to legalise surrogate motherhood and permit late-term abortions of up to 22 weeks in some hospitals.

The party has teamed up with JA21 to form a right-wing block of 12 seats, which would be enough to give the coalition a majority in the Lower House. However, they would still be short in the Senate, where any right-wing majority depends on the support of the farmers’ party BBB.

BBB key

The BBB has not been invited to the talks so far because of its staunch opposition to the cabinet’s plans to reduce nitrogen pollution, which would require some livestock farmers to give up or drastically reduce the size of their herds.

Party leader Henk Vermeer is meeting Heinen on Tuesday, but the BBB is not expected to compromise on its stance. “Anyone who can count can see they can’t do without us”.

The 20 seats held by Pro would give the cabinet a clear majority in the lower house, while only one small party such as Volt would be needed to pass the budget in the Senate.

But the right-wing VVD is reluctant to rely solely on Klaver’s party, which was kept out of the coalition in February on the insistence of VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz.

World.title: Dutch cocaine-broker case in Colombia grows to 55 suspects
World.content:
An investigation into two Dutch men accused of brokering cocaine shipments from Colombia has grown into a much wider case, with prosecutors now pursuing 55 suspects, 35 of them already arrested, for drug trafficking, money laundering, extortion, violence and planned kidnappings.

Pre-trial hearings began on Monday at Zwolle district court, broadcaster NOS reported. The two main suspects, Dutch men aged 42 and 47, were arrested in Colombia in February and are still awaiting extradition, which can take more than a year.

The case grew out of a national police investigation opened in January 2025. Prosecutors say the pair connected Colombian cartels with cocaine buyers in the Netherlands and arranged shipments of hundreds of kilos at a time.

Intercepted chat messages then led investigators to a web of associates, and twelve further investigations are now running.

One concerns four men who allegedly prepared to kidnap the girlfriend of a man suspected of stealing a cocaine shipment in 2024, a theft that left a debt of more than €700,000. The kidnapping did not go ahead, and prosecutors say they do not know why.

Another involves two men accused of extorting around 1,000 clients of the sex-work website Kinky, who allegedly faced threats of serious violence unless they paid. Police believe the pair took more than €100,000.

The Netherlands has invested heavily in police cooperation with Colombia, which prosecutors say is now producing results, with several Dutch nationals arrested there. The main suspects’ cases will not be heard in full until they are extradited

World.title: Health inspectors ban webshop from selling weight loss drugs
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Health inspectors have banned a website from selling unlicensed weight loss drugs that it advertised on social media.

De Peptidekoning sold two medicines prescribed to treat diabetes, semaglutide and tirzepatide, and a third, retatrutide, which is an experimental drug that has not been licensed in any country.

The Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) ordered the owners of the website to stop selling all three substances and warned patients not to risk their health with experimental treatments.

It said De Peptidekoning, which trades through several websites including puritybase.com, did not have a license to sell the medicines. “They have not adequately ensured that the medicines meet standards for quality, safety and effectiveness,” the IGJ said.

“The way in which the medicines were offered for sale does not give enough reassurances, which creates risks for public health.”

RTL Nieuws reported that unauthorised traders were profiting from a black market in slimming treatments for people who were not prescribed medicines such as Ozempic, which are only available in the Netherlands to treat diabetes.

Marloes Dankers, of the Utrecht-based Dutch Institute for the Rational Use of Medicine, an advisory body set up by doctors and pharmacists, said: “People are making guinea-pigs of themselves.

“These medicines are still being researched and we don’t know what exactly the risks are. That’s the reason for doing the research.”

Eli Lilly, the American manufacturer developing retratrutide, also urged people not to buy the drug online.

“What is being sold on the black market is not a medicine, it has not been approved or verified in any way and it is not worth the risk,” the company said.

World.title: Both Dutch teams reach hockey World Cup semi-finals
World.content:
The Dutch men’s hockey team moved into the semi-finals of the World Cup in Amstelveen on Monday evening with a 2-2 draw against England in what was a tense and physical game.

The Dutch needed at least a draw to be sure of progressing to the next round, while England were chasing a win by a two-goal margin.

Playing in bright sunlight in a packed Wagener Stadium, England opened the scoring after five minutes, with the Dutch equalising with just 40 seconds remaining before the end of the first half.

England went into the lead again 90 seconds into the second half but the Netherlands drew level once more. England took off their goalkeeper with seven minutes to go, but despite piling on the pressure, the Dutch kept them at bay, much to the delight of the largely orange-clad crowd.

The 2-2 draw was enough to put the Netherlands at the top of their group, with Argentina, who beat India 5-3, in second place. The Netherlands will now meet Spain in the semi-finals in Amstelveen on Friday, while Argentina will play Germany in Belgium, which is co-hosting the tournament.

In the women’s competition, the Netherlands are hot favourites and will meet Belgium in the first semi-final on Thursday at the Wagener Stadium. They beat China 4-1 on Sunday to reach the next stage. Argentina will play Spain in Belgium.

World.title: NS offers cheaper tickets to ease busy morning trains
World.content:
NS is making some rush-hour train tickets cheaper from Tuesday, in an effort to ease its busiest morning services and free up seats.

The national rail operator is extending its PrijsTijd Deals – advance-purchase tickets that give a discount for travelling on quieter trains – to the edges of the morning peak. Discounts there will average around 30%, against up to 60% in the quietest off-peak hours. The tickets must be bought at least a day ahead.

The move is separate from the €49 summer pass for unlimited off-peak travel, which runs until September 1. It is also exactly the same as an earlier NS plan to add a surcharge to peak fares, which MPs blocked in 2023.

NS says the crush is worst on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, when large numbers of passengers travel within a single hour. Nudging even a fraction of them onto a train 15 or 30 minutes earlier or later, it argues, spreads the load and means more people get a seat.

“The NS, like electricity grid operators for example, has to deal with peak load,” said NS timetabling director Tijmen Voet. “But if a small percentage of travellers choose a less busy alternative, passengers have to stand far less often.”

Limited reach

Rail passengers’ association Rover welcomed the extension but said more was needed to make a real difference. It has long argued the discounts should also be bookable on the day of travel, rather than only up to a day ahead.

The reach is likely to stay limited, a Rover spokesperson said, because many hyper-peak travellers hold season tickets paid for by their employer and feel no price incentive. Others cannot shift their journey because of fixed school or work hours.

An NS trial last year found a fifth of passengers would take a quieter train in return for a discount, with most willing to wait up to half an hour. That, Voet said, lets the operator run fewer long trains for peak crowds that otherwise travel largely empty for the rest of the day.

Polish state defence firm Mesko has signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.9 billion) agreement to supply its Piorun man-portable air-defence systems to the armed forces of Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia. The deal is being financed through the European Union’s SAFE mechanism. The agreement represents the largest-ever purchase of Pioruns, which have become an export hit for Mesko after proving their worth during Ukraine’s defence against Russian aggression. Previous buyers include Sweden, the United States, Belgium, Estonia and Norway itself. Nowy etap #PolskaSAFE. Rozpoczynamy wspólne zakupy i to znów w polskim przemyśle! To jak to było,… pic.twitter.com/YIDWBGBvpm — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) August 24, 2026 The deal will see the firm provide “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles for its shoulder-fired Piorun systems, which target low-flying aircraft such as planes, helicopters and drones. Over 80% will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, with the remainder going to its three NATO allies. The purchase is being funded through SAFE, which provides loans at preferential terms for defence spending. While SAFE can be used individually by countries to make purchases for their own armed forces, some funds are designated for joint procurement by groups of countries (including non-EU member Norway). “Our partners from Lithuania, Latvia and Norway have decided to purchase from Poland,” declared deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who oversees Poland’s participation in SAFE. “We are a leader in the SAFE mechanism and are the first to create such agreements. For the first time, the [Polish defence ministry’s] Armaments Agency is making purchases not only for the Polish armed forces, but also for those of our allies.” “This is a measure of the success of the Polish arms industry,” declared defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, as the deal was announced on Monday. “This is the moment when Poland can proudly say: we are a European leader.” He noted that Mesko’s production capacity is now 2.5 times larger than it was when the current government took power in December 2023. Since SAFE launched in May, the firm’s staffing, which stood at 3,200 by the end of last year, has increased by around 200, added the minister. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. However, the programme has been opposed by the right-wing opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argue that it will give Brussels too much influence over Polish defence spending and burden Poland with decades of debt on uncertain terms. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. World.title: Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski seeks to switch allegiance to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A rising US track star has declared his intention to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. Sam Blaskowski’s personal-best 100 metres sprint time of 9.89 seconds is more than a tenth of a second faster than the current Polish national record. “I plan to make Poland the finest sprinting nation in the world. I want to win medals for Poland,” the 23-year-old told Polish broadcaster TVP Sport. Sam Blaskowski przed naszymi kamerami mówi o tym, dlaczego chciałby reprezentować Polskę! 🇵🇱 Więcej o tej sprawie 👉 https://t.co/oC8MJ4moV6 pic.twitter.com/Nw1i7YqrIp — TVP SPORT (@sport_tvppl) August 23, 2026 Blaskowski says that two of his ancestors, Franciszek and Julian, left Poland in 1905, at a time when the country was still partitioned between Germany, Austria and Russia. “My last name is Polish. But for a long time, I didn’t understand that these were my roots. Everything changed recently, because my parents and I talked a lot about our roots,” he explained to TVP Sport. He was contacted by Piotr Maruszewski, coach of the Polish sprint team, after clocking a time of 9.89 seconds in May, which is the joint-ninth-best run by anyone in the world this year. The Polish 100m record is still held by Marian Woronin, who ran 10.00 in 1984. View this post on Instagram A post shared by D3 Glory Days | D3 Running Podcast & News (@d3glorydays) Maruszewski has since been persuading and helping Blaskowski to apply for citizenship, including hiring lawyers to obtain documents proving the sprinter’s heritage. Under Polish law, people who have a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who was born in or lived in Poland after January 1920 are themselves regarded as holding Polish citizenship. That means Blaskowski’s ancestry may not be enough to qualify. However, it could be enough to convince Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has discretion to grant citizenship to anyone he wishes. Last year, Nawrocki granted citizenship to Vladimir Semirunniy, a speed skater who fled from Russia to Poland. Semirunniy now represents the Polish national team, including at this year’s Winter Olympics, where he won a silver medal. Given that Blaskowski last represented the United States as a junior over four years ago, he is not subject to World Athletics’ mandatory waiting period for athletes transferring national allegiance. At yesterday’s Silesia Diamond League meeting in Chorzów, Poland’s biggest annual athletics event, Blaskowski told Citius Mag that he expects to be able to represent Poland at next year’s World Championships in Beijing. “I want to inspire the next generation… to make an impact on people around me, and I think the best way to do that is to go and represent Poland,” he told TVP Sport at the same event. “Not only do I have heritage there, but people [in Poland] are very aware of your talent and they give so much appreciation for our sport, and I think it’s a great place.” He added that he and his parents plan to visit their ancestors’ hometown of Sompolno in central Poland on Monday before he again competes in Szczecin on Wednesday. In Chorzów, Blaskowski came fifth in his semi-final against some of the world’s sprinters, just ahead of European champion Romell Glave. Poland’s current top male sprinter, Dominik Kopeć, finished ninth and last in 10.32. The final was won by Jamaica’s Oblique Seville in 9.83 seconds, ahead of another American with a Polish surname, Kenneth Bednarek, who was adopted as a child by a woman with Polish heritage. “The love and support I received from Poland today were truly incredible,” Bednarek wrote on social media after competing at the same event two years ago. “I’m thrilled to have run here for the first time and can’t wait to return with my mom, who has Polish roots.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kung Fu Kenny (@kenny_bednarek) Blaskowski would not be the first sprinter to switch allegiance to Poland. Belarusian runner Krystsina Tsimanouskaya received Polish citizenship in 2022, having been granted a humanitarian visa the previous year after the Tokyo Olympics. This month, high jumper Maria Żodzik, another Belarusian who was granted Polish citizenship in 2024, won silver at the European Championships, adding to another silver at last year’s World Championships. At the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, Poland’s athletes disappointed, finishing with just one bronze medal in track and field events and one gold and ten medals overall, the country’s worst result since 1956. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
