World.title: Tigress Umit Shows Signs of Successful Adaptation in Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – Tigress Umit, released into Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on July 31 as part of the country’s tiger reintroduction program, is showing positive signs of adapting to the wild, Anuarbek Bermagambetov, head of the Department of Hunting Management and Wildlife, said on the Jibek Joly TV channel on Aug. 24.

More than 70 years after tigers disappeared from Kazakhstan, the predator has returned as part of a long-term reintroduction effort.

Umit’s first recorded prey was a wolf, followed several days later by a wild boar. According to Bermagambetov, her hunting behavior in the first 10 days suggests she is adapting well to her new environment.

Her movements are monitored around the clock with a GPS tracker that transmits her location and direction of travel every 12 hours. Specialists still need to conduct field visits to identify the prey species she catches, as GPS data alone cannot determine this.

Strict monitoring and safety measures

The tigress is currently staying within the reserve’s designated green zone, which covers her main habitat and hunting grounds and poses no immediate threat to nearby settlements.

The reserve covers more than 450,000 hectares, and unauthorized access is prohibited.

The area around Umit has been divided into green, yellow and red zones. If she moves towards the yellow zone, a specially formed conflict-management team will begin monitoring the situation. The team is equipped with three vehicles, a snowmobile, an ATV, night-vision devices, a satellite phone and Starlink.

If Umit enters the red zone, authorities will issue an alert and notify residents of nearby settlements through mobile warnings.

Specialists will initially attempt to drive the tiger back into the green zone using sound and, if necessary, pyrotechnic devices. Temporary sedation is also available as a last resort.

Reintroduction program underway since 2010

Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program has been underway since 2010. The project has included establishing the Ile-Balkhash reserve, restoring its wildlife population and developing the infrastructure needed to support the species’ return.

Two tigers, Bogdan and Puma, were previously brought from the Netherlands in 2024, while Russia transferred four more tigers to Kazakhstan this year. Umit is one of the four animals Russia sent under a bilateral agreement.

Before her release, specialists assessed the reserve’s food base. The area is home to potential tiger prey, including kulan, wild boar, roe deer and Bukhara deer.

Authorities say Umit’s ability to hunt and feed independently is an encouraging early sign that the tigress is adapting to life in the wild.

Officials have also urged the public not to rely on unverified social media footage. Videos of Bogdan and Puma have previously been falsely circulated as footage of Umit, highlighting the growing problem of AI-generated and misleading wildlife content online.

World.title: Adilet Wins Kurultai Elections with 71.17% of Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party secured a landslide victory in Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections, winning 71.17% of the vote and 110 seats, according to the final results announced by the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Aug. 25.

The electoral rolls included 12,623,289 voters, and 9,351,539 cast ballots. Voter turnout stood at 74.08%.

Adilet received 6,528,948 votes (71.17%) and secured 110 seats in the Kurultai. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party won 574,621 votes (6.26%) and 10 seats, while Respublica received 509,631 votes (5.56%) and secured nine seats.

The Aq Zhol Democratic Party garnered 478,083 votes (5.21%) and eight seats. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party received 469,058 votes (5.11%) and also secured eight seats.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes (3.11%), while the Baytaq Green Party garnered 97,751 votes (1.07%). Both parties failed to clear the statutory 5% electoral threshold.

A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.

Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, political parties must secure at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats in the Kurultai. Five parties crossed the threshold based on the final results.

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system. The 145-member Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament under the Constitution that took effect July 1.

World.title: Nigeria, Sierra Leone See Sharp Rise in Business Registrations in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – The number of companies with founders from Nigeria and Sierra Leone registered in Kazakhstan increased sharply in July.

The number of Nigerian-founded companies rose by 68, while companies with founders from Sierra Leone rose by 45, the Data Hub analytical Telegram channel reported on Aug. 14.

The figures come as Kazakhstan expands economic engagement with African countries. Trade, logistics, agriculture, mining, investment and digital technologies are among the areas of cooperation. Kazakhstan is also developing a Strategy for Cooperation with African States and the African Union for 2025-2030.

Nigeria remains African leader

The number of companies with Nigerian founders increased from 359 on July 1 to 427 on Aug. 1, a 19% rise.

Nigeria has the largest number of registered companies in Kazakhstan among African countries and ranks 21st among all countries represented in the registry.

All Nigerian-founded companies are classified as small businesses. Education accounts for 56% of the total. The July increase came mainly from the “provision of other services” category, which added 61 companies. The latest rise follows an earlier increase in 2023, while the number of Nigerian companies declined in 2024 and 2025.

Sierra Leone sees 2.5-fold increase

Companies with Sierra Leonean founders increased from 30 on July 1 to 75 on Aug. 1. The 45 new registrations exceeded the total number recorded at the beginning of July.

The increase was concentrated in the “provision of other services” category, which went from zero to 44 companies. Education accounted for 20 organizations, up by one during the month.

World.title: Kazakhstan Introduces AI Analytics in Transport Sector
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s AI platform Echelon Alpha presented the government with its artificial intelligence capabilities for real-time analysis of markets, transport routes and cross-sector economic links.

The presentation took place on Aug. 24 at the Situational Center of the Ministry of Transport of Kazakhstan, where Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov reviewed the implementation of the President’s instructions on the digitalization of the transport sector and the latest IT solutions being introduced. Echelon Alpha was presented among the digital technologies being implemented in the transport sector.

“President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has identified the further development of a digital services state as a priority. Digitalization and artificial intelligence must deliver tangible benefits to citizens, businesses and the state. The government faces the task of accelerating the implementation of practical AI solutions across all sectors of the economy. I instruct that the projects presented today for the technological transformation of the transport sector be fully implemented nationwide as soon as possible,” Bektenov said.

One of the key areas of Echelon Alpha is aviation. The system models a prospective network of direct and transit flights through Kazakhstan, assessing demand, economics and route competitiveness. The model has been trained on data from approximately 200 million flights across 190 hubs and aggregates information from more than 70 open sources. Cross-checking against government databases showed an accuracy rate of 95%.

“Echelon Alpha uses AI to analyze market dynamics in real time and provide a basis for fast and accurate decisions. This is a joint project with the Ministry of Transport: the system builds an optimal network and forecasts the commercial viability of any destination,” said Rakhman Asambayev, CEO of Echelon Alpha.

The platform also enables a detailed analysis of the economics of individual flight paths. For example, when modeling the Hyderabad–Astana–Moscow сonnection, the system takes into account more than 170 airline reports, up-to-date ticket and fuel price data, and compares the potential route with existing connections.

The analysis goes beyond commercial viability to assess the broader economic impact of developing the aviation network, including direct and indirect revenues, tax contributions and wider effects on the economy. According to the presented estimates, the potential overall impact could reach 70 billion tenge (US$154 million) per year, while the estimated economic impact of a single passenger is approximately $25.

However, aviation is only one of the platform’s capabilities. At the core of the system is the Echelon analytical engine, which integrates data from different sectors and models their interdependencies. For example, changes in oil refining volumes can affect the country’s fuel balance, tax revenues, transport and other sectors of the economy. The digital solution enables these effects to be assessed in advance and different development scenarios to be modeled.

Thus, Echelon Alpha transforms large-scale data into real-time scenario analysis, helping decision-makers assess risks more quickly, identify new opportunities and make informed decisions while taking into account the interconnections between different sectors.

The prime minister also instructed the government to strengthen the integration of information systems across the transport sector and related industries to improve safety, reduce processing times and optimize costs. The implementation of analytical solutions can contribute to more effective use of data, faster analysis of changes and improved decision-making.

World.title: Observers Call for Improvements After Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first election to the new unicameral Kurultai marked a significant stage in the country’s constitutional reform, according to international assessments released after the Aug. 23 vote. An OSCE-led mission found the process technically well prepared but said political competition remained limited.

The International Election Observation Mission presented its preliminary findings in Astana on Aug. 24. It brought together the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (OSCE PA) and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), deploying 339 observers from 43 countries.

The mission said the campaign and election day were generally calm and orderly and that contestants were provided equal conditions to organize campaign activities. It also cited the range of political parties participating, the absence of independent parliamentary candidacies and differences in party resources as factors affecting the level of political competition.

“The elections took place at an important moment for Kazakhstan in the continuation of reforms initiated from 2019, which culminated in this year’s constitutional referendum. After undertaking a constitutional reset of its electoral framework, Kazakhstan’s early parliamentary elections provided an opportunity to see whether these changes opened space for healthy political competition,” said Gábor Hajdu, OSCE Special Co-ordinator and leader of the short-term observer mission. “Despite some positive aspects, there are few genuine opportunities for independent candidacies, limited space for civil society and the independent media, and a lack of a level playing field consistent with OSCE commitments, including for women,” he added.

Political competition and new electoral framework

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary vote under the Constitution that entered into force July 1. The new 145-member Kurultai is elected for five years through closed-list proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency with a 5% electoral threshold.

Seven political parties contested the election with 545 registered candidates. Party platforms addressed a range of social and economic issues, although the mission noted that all contesting parties supported President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s policies.

The mission also examined the position of Adilet, which merged with the former ruling Amanat party ahead of the election. Observers said Adilet drew on Amanat’s organizational structures, networks and resources and ran the most extensive and visible campaign. The mission also reported instances involving the use of administrative resources during campaign activities and said these circumstances affected the balance of competition

Lucija Tacer Perlin, head of the OSCE PA delegation, said the wider political environment was important alongside the administration of the vote.

“The absence of parties representing genuine political opposition and the elimination of the right to stand independently for parliamentary elections limited political participation, pluralism, and electoral competitiveness. While party platforms and campaign messages addressed a wide range of social and economic issues, all contesting parties supported the incumbent president’s policies. We also observed that a number of factors affected the level playing field during the campaign,” she said.

The preliminary assessment also addressed political parties’ role in determining who ultimately receives seats in the Kurultai. Some ODIHR interlocutors from local party branches raised questions about the transparency of how lists are compiled and how parties subsequently determine which candidates take seats.

The law maintains a cumulative 30% quota for women, youth and persons with disabilities both on candidate lists and when mandates are distributed. Some 43.9% of registered candidates belonged to at least one of those groups. According to the mission, the combined quota does not guarantee effective representation of each group separately.

Election administration and voting

The mission assessed the technical administration of the election broadly positively, saying election commissions prepared for the vote professionally and within legal deadlines, conducted nationwide training and voter-information campaigns, and took steps to improve accessibility for voters with disabilities. It also noted that contesting parties generally expressed confidence in the election administration.

Election day was described as calm and orderly. International observers assessed opening and voting as overwhelmingly in line with procedures, with voting receiving a positive assessment in 98% of the 1,327 polling stations observed.

Ambassador Vincent Piket, head of the ODIHR election observation mission, said that while much of election day proceeded well, observers identified shortcomings in voting and counting procedures, including discrepancies between observed voter activity and official turnout data.

“While much went well, observers noted a number of serious procedural shortcomings. For instance, they saw identical signatures of voter lists, they saw a lack of enforcement of proper identification requirements by voters, aspiring voters, they saw a non-respect of the secrecy of the casting of ballots, and photographs were taken of ballots in the ballot box and around it. And there were also marked differences between voter activity on the one hand and official turnout data on the other,” said Piket.

Media and public participation

The mission said voters had access to a wide range of media outlets, while noting limited pluralism in the media environment. ODIHR monitoring found that contestants were generally covered in a neutral tone, though election reporting included relatively little analytical or in-depth coverage.

PACE delegation head Sevilay Çelenk said the assessment went beyond election-day procedures to consider the broader conditions for political participation, including media access, political pluralism and public confidence in electoral institutions.

“The relationship between elections and democracy is more delicate than it appears. No democracy can exist without elections, yet the presence of elections doesn’t by itself guarantee democracy. What matters is not just the ballot box, it is also what surrounds it. Campaigns must be free, media access must be equal, institutions must be independent. Political pluralism must be protected. Citizens must trust that their votes will be counted honestly,” said Çelenk.

Broader international perspectives

Additional international commentary on the election focused on the broader constitutional transition and Kazakhstan’s development agenda.

James Whitney, CEO of Car Park Transformer (CPT), welcomed the constitutional reforms and said the company’s infrastructure projects are aligned with Kazakhstan’s broader development priorities and its position between major East-West trade and transport routes.

Honorary Consul of Kazakhstan in Iceland Sigurður Atli Jónsson described the first election to the unicameral Kurultai as a milestone in Kazakhstan’s political development, saying the new framework could bring greater institutional clarity and predictability for international partners and businesses.

“Constitutional reform of this scale is rare, and carrying it through to a new legislature marks the completion of a process that has been years in the making. Seen from Reykjavík, what stands out is the direction of travel,” said Jónsson.

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.
