Tech.title: The County Prosecutors Who Became ICE Informants
Tech.content:
This story was produced in partnership with Injustice Watch, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago focused on the court system.

Rolando Perez Samayoa had come to the US in 2023 seeking safety. Fleeing violence in Mexico, he’d first planned to make a life in Alabama but had been told that Illinois would protect immigrants like him. “There’s some kind of law there,” he said. “It’s supposed to be a sanctuary.”

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

He was referring to the state’s 2017 TRUST Act, which was meant to keep local law enforcement out of federal deportation efforts. Samayoa made his way to southern Illinois and found work cleaning a factory. After a DUI arrest in Marion County last October, Samayoa said, he attended his hearings—a fact confirmed by court records.

In late January, John Christeson, an assistant state’s attorney in the office prosecuting the case, emailed an agent with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, about Samayoa. The message included his date of birth, an upcoming court date, and where he lived: Centralia, Illinois.

“Ok, we’ll take care of it, thank you,” the federal agent, Sergio Fulgencio, wrote back minutes later. Two days later, he wanted to know more: “Do you have any reports on this guy?”

Christeson sent him the police report and related tickets. Three weeks later, federal agents apprehended Samayoa outside his home. They hauled off his 17-year-old son, too.

The exchange is among dozens of emails reviewed by Injustice Watch that reveal a pattern of consequential collaboration between county prosecutors and federal immigration agencies across Illinois during the first 15 months of President Donald Trump’s second term.

State’s attorneys offices in 1 out of every 6 Illinois counties acted as valuable assets of federal immigration enforcement, sharing sensitive personal data about the people they were prosecuting without criminal warrants, public disclosure, or legislative oversight and with no accounting of how often it happened or who was affected.

Tech.title: Optoma GT2400HDR Review: Ace Projector for Golf Simulation
Tech.content:
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.

I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.

Made for Indoor Driving Ranges

Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)

Tech.title: Border Wall Construction Threatens 6,000 Years of History on Private Lands
Tech.content:
Outrage has exploded over border infrastructure that recently began tearing up pristine desert landscapes in Big Bend National Park. But there’s a quieter battle taking place on private lands in Texas, where the US border wall is set to cut across some of North America's richest archaeological sites, digging up ancient indigenous artifacts and fracturing millennia-old rock art in its path.

The US Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection awarded billions of dollars in contracts this year toward the construction of a wall and other barriers in West Texas along a remote 500-plus-mile (800-plus-kilometer) riverfront expanse of the US-Mexico border that includes Big Bend National Park and other idyllic parklands.

Bipartisan backlash against border wall construction in the national park was swift, ultimately prompting DHS to scuttle plans for a 30-foot steel bollard wall, instead replacing it with miles of riverside vehicle barriers and 200-plus miles of road construction. Bulldozers began clearing along the Rio Grande corridor near Santa Elena Canyon on August 6.

Construction has since been paused in the park in response to lawsuits. But the agency is still planning to construct the wall, as well as a web of road construction, over mountains and across canyons outside the national park. That includes private property that ranchers and other landowners say have archeological sites worth protecting, too. And they’re concerned that construction of the wall will bifurcate their own land and damage archeological sites, many of which have yet to be fully studied.

Archeologist Bryon Schroeder has been digging on rancher Jeff Fort’s property for two years. Schroeder runs Sul Ross University’s Center for Big Bend Studies, a research program dedicated to studying the cultural, historical, and archeological legacy of the region. He removes 4 inches (10 centimeters) of sediment at a time, and his meticulous digs have uncovered pottery and melted adobe slick building material from as early as the year AD 800. He’s found turquoise, too, and marine shells, both signs of trade outside the region. Evidence shows the site is related to Paquimé, an UNESCO World Heritage site that’s 200 miles away in Mexico.

Schroeder’s dig site, Canta Recio, is directly in the path of the proposed wall. Some of it is set to be bulldozed over. If the wall is built, other parts of the site will also become effectively inaccessible.

Schroeder likens Canta Recio to how Egyptians set up shop along the Nile, surmising the site was settled four or five times between 800 and 1400 by groups who were likely drawn to fertile land afforded by routine floods. Of course, those floods also mean that groups were eventually forced to move on when the Rio Grande overtopped its banks, only for another group to eventually settle the area once the silt firmed up. A settlement, a flood, an exit, on repeat.

“There's some bigger, cooler sites up the river that are just insane,” Schroeder said. “They have so much pottery, they have Mesoamerican copper bells, they have turquoise. They have all sorts of crazy stuff.”

The paradox facing Schroeder and other archeologists: They can't fully measure what's at risk because many of the archeological sites exist on private ranches and have never been studied.

That means construction may erase history before anyone gets to record it. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told WIRED that the agency is conducting environmental and cultural reviews to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.

But previous studies haven’t stopped historically important sites from being sentenced to destruction. A 30-foot bollard wall is set to go right through the Polvo site, in Redford, Texas, which is home to a prehistoric village complete with burial ground dating back to the 1300s. The same site also has evidence of a Spanish mission that was built in the 1600s. Eagle Nest Canyon in Langtry, one of the most significant and intensively studied archeological sites in all of Texas, is also slated to see some form of barrier erected through it. That site includes the southernmost bison jump site in the US, where Native Americans hunted the animals en masse by funneling them over a cliff.

Tech.title: It Should Be Harder to Apply for a Job. No, Really
Tech.content:
Three years ago, Andrew Stockwell had his hiring routine down to a science.

As head of people for the software-buying company Vendr, Stockwell posted a listing, waited a few days, and then reviewed a few dozen applications—up to 100, if he was lucky. Recruiters identified other potential candidates, adding a few more applicants to the mix. Stockwell read résumés, conducted interviews, and passed along sterling candidates to hiring managers.

“It was really about finding that great talent, sussing out that talent, speaking with that talent, and identifying the best possible people,” Stockwell tells WIRED.

Sometime in the last year or so, Stockwell says, everything changed. The process started off the same way, but within a day or two, Stockwell wasn’t looking at 100 candidates. Instead, he was flooded with hundreds of applications. Sometimes, the incoming topped a thousand. A good chunk were “total bogus,” Stockwell says—fake candidates. Many more appeared to have been written using artificial intelligence, stretching the truth and making it difficult to distinguish one applicant from another. The sheer quantity was overwhelming. Stockwell says he found himself “paying my talent-acquisition professionals—who are high-paid, high-quality individuals—just to look through applications all day long.”

Stockwell is one of many recruitment professionals who believe looking for a job is fundamentally broken. In 2026, job hunting has become as easy as online shopping: AI can crank out tailored résumés and cover letters in seconds. Browser extensions can autofill applications, no human necessary. LinkedIn serves users dozens of jobs a day, many with the option to apply with “just a few clicks.”

“A year ago, every recruiter would tell me: We want to make it as easy as possible to apply for jobs,” offering candidates a “seamless experience,” Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI for Greenhouse, tells WIRED. Samson joined the recruiting platform earlier this year, when it acquired his startup, which used AI to conduct job interviews. “What they got was 2,000 applicants in 24 hours for a job. That is a shitty experience for everyone.”

Good applicants can’t stand out, while bad candidates slip through the cracks. Recruiters, Samson says, face the tortuous task of judging thousands of candidates, every single day. Instead of taking the time to search LinkedIn for dream employees, they spend hours in applicant tracking systems, tweaking filters to try to determine whose applications are worth a 30-second skim.

Tech.title: Spirit Airlines Wants to Sell Its Data to Google. Former Flight Attendants Are Freaked Out
Tech.content:
Spirit Airlines may have declared bankruptcy this spring, but the budget airline is still worth something—to AI giants, at least. In mid-August, Google won a $10 million bid to purchase some 34 years of the airline’s data, from invoices and flight operations information to Wi-Fi sales, employee records, and crew pairings.

In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge.

If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems.

The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!”

The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI.

Tech.title: Omega Just Released a Mini Moonwatch
Tech.content:
I have skinny wrists. So skinny, in fact, that during the craze from the late 1990s to early 2010s, when watch cases started to tip over 48 mm, it became hard to find pieces that suited those of us not blessed (or cursed) with Schwarzenegger-sized forearms. Thankfully, watch case sizes have calmed down considerably since then, and now it's easy to find smaller models, particularly around that 38- to 40-mm Goldilocks zone.

This brings us neatly to Omega's latest collection of Speedmasters, all of which come in that ideal 38-mm size. The seven references in new color variations have been tweaked to improve the existing 38-mm Speedy collection. The most notable improvement? The oval subdials have been banished in favor of proper rounded versions seen on the Moonwatch. The bezels have also been overhauled in Moonwatch style and are now thicker with the essential Dot-Over-Ninety.

Tech.title: CNET Finds 75% of US Adults Couldn’t Care Less About a Foldable iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple could release its first foldable iPhone in a few weeks at the company’s annual September event (which could be Sept. 9). The late summer showcase is usually Apple’s big reveal for new hardware. The center of attention could be the rumored iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first foldable.

Analysts say the phone could be dubbed the iPhone Ultra (previously nicknamed the iPhone Fold and iPhone Flip). It’s expected to be a tiny iPad that folds in half, into a regular-size iPhone when closed. Rumors suggest Apple’s folding phone will feature a wide book-style fold, similar to the original Google Pixel Fold and the recently released Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a folding display with the same aspect ratio as an iPad.

The iPhone Ultra could also have two rear-facing and a single front-facing camera that works whether it’s folded or not, and come with Apple’s usual features and services. Analysts expect the phone to cost between $2,000 and $2,500, which is on par with, if not a little higher than, rival folding phones from Motorola, Google and Samsung.

However, most US adults say they aren’t interested in buying a new foldable phone.

A CNET survey that polled 2,605 US adults found that 75% aren’t interested in buying a foldable Apple device. Even if they bought one, they wouldn’t shell out thousands of dollars for it.

Key takeaways

Three out of four US adults (75%) are indifferent about buying a foldable Apple device, such as the rumored Apple iPhone Ultra.

US adults would spend an average of $781 on an Apple foldable device, which is a stark contrast to what analysts say the phone could cost (and $48 less than the base model iPhone 17).

The RAM shortage is affecting nearly half (41%) of US adults’ plans to upgrade their phones. Some are holding onto their current devices longer than originally planned.

Most US adults don’t want a foldable iPhone

CNET found that most US adults, regardless of age, aren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. Older generations (Boomers and Gen X) express the least interest — 83% and 77%, respectively. Younger generations aren’t that excited either, with nearly 70% of Gen Z and millennials (69% and 68%, respectively) not interested in a foldable iPhone. And those who are excited about one aren’t willing to break the bank for it.

Cole Kan/CNET

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, finds it surprising that only 75% weren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. “Foldable phones are niche products, and it’s impressive that 25% might be interested in an Apple folding phone,” said Holland. “That would be a killer product debut if Apple could get that many people to buy one.”

The same thing can be said for the iPhone Mini and Plus models for those who want a smaller or larger screen, but still want an iPhone. Or the E series, which is a budget-friendly model starting at $600 before discounts.

Holland pointed out that the foldable iPhone isn’t meant to replace the baseline model; it’s about expanding the line and offering phone models at an even bigger price range. Apple could have an iPhone model at ever $100 increase between $600 and $2,000.

US adults will spend an average of $781 on a new foldable iPhone

On average, US adults are willing to spend $781 on a new foldable iPhone. That’s less than what most iPhones cost now. For context, the base model of the iPhone 17 starts at $799 (with a $30 carrier discount).

Gen Z is willing to spend the most on a foldable iPhone — an average of $919 — whereas other generations would spend less. Millennials would spend an average of $859, Gen X would spend $690, and Boomers even less — $572.

Cole Kan/CNET

“The fact that people want an average price that’s nearly $50 below the baseline iPhone 17 shows where we’re at financially right now,” said Holland. “A foldable iPhone is going to be expensive to make, and its retail price will likely reflect that.”

But foldable phones haven’t always been this expensive. Holland points out that the price of foldable phones has dropped for years, as with the Motorola Razr line. The first model cost $1,400, but last year you could buy a new one for half that price before discounts. Now those prices have started to rise again (because of the RAM shortage), and the rumored $2,000 price for the iPhone Ultra is proof of that. It’s a few hundred dollars more than foldable phones cost just a couple of years ago, Holland said.

The RAM shortage is affecting iPhone upgrade plans

The evolution of AI and data centers has led to a memory chip shortage — also known as the RAM shortage or RAMageddon. Personal devices, like phones and laptops, need those chips for data storage. However, the shortage has led tech companies to raise prices on their devices.

Apple raised prices on many of its devices in June for this very reason. The RAM shortage and price increases are making 41% US adults rethink their plans to upgrade to a new iPhone — regardless of whether it’s a foldable or another model.

“The very companies investing in AI and building data centers to support new features and tools on phones are the ones passing the higher cost of RAM and chips on to consumers,” said Holland. “There’s a corporate Gift of the Magi happening, and it’s us who are footing the bill while companies rake in record-breaking profits.”

Many contemplating an upgrade are weighing other options due to price increases. Some are considering older or less expensive options (5%) and switching to another brand (4%), while others are considering refurbished or used models (4%) to save money on the upgrade. Others (9%) will only upgrade if a trade-in or a mobile carrier promotion covers the price, which usually comes in the form of account credits or a multiyear commitment to stay with that carrier.

The bigger story is that most US adults aren’t eager to upgrade due to the RAM shortage and device price hikes. Ten percent are planning to delay their upgrade and keep their phone longer, while 9% are holding onto their phone longer than originally planned.

Twenty-two percent of US adults don’t plan to upgrade anytime soon, regardless of Apple’s new devices or the impact of the RAM shortage. By generation, 19% of Gen X and 27% of Boomers don’t have plans to upgrade anytime soon, while 16% of millennials and 21% of Gen Zers share the same sentiment. Here’s a breakdown.

If you have an old phone and the battery is the only issue, replace it instead of getting a new phone, Holland said. “You’ll add another two to three years of life onto your phone and avoid paying hundreds of dollars more for an upgrade or multiyear commitment to a carrier.”

If you’re still thinking of upgrading your phone, Holland said the best deals on phones are typically found when a new model launches or during holiday sales. And even though trading in your old phone is a good way to save money, check with third-party reseller sites, too.

“You might be able to get more money for your old phone than from the carrier or phone-maker is offering,” said Holland. “Used and refurbished phones are definitely worth buying, as are models from a year or two ago, and often discounted by hundreds.”

Lastly, be skeptical about that “free” $1,000-plus phone a carrier is willing to give you. These deals often come with multiyear commitments and are shown as account credit rather than cash. If you switch to a new mobile carrier before the phone is paid off, you’ll have to pay the difference.

Methodology

All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,605 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Aug. 13 and 17, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

Tech.title: The Best Smart Home Devices for Your Desk or Office
Tech.content:
The humble home desk needs smart features, too. Here’s where to begin. Getty Images

I frequently discuss smart home devices for the kitchen, front door or even the bedroom, but there’s one home space I sometimes forget to talk about: the home desk. Whether you have a simple computer setup in the corner or a dedicated office, your desk could use smart upgrades, too.

Here, I’m going through my favorite picks for a home desk and why they’re so handy, starting with something every home should have.

A smart surge protector to protect all your other devices

Meross has extra cord length if you need to do more positioning with your power strip. Meross/CNET

A strong surge protector is the glue that holds all the other desk devices together — and protects them from dangerous electrical surges. I have a full list of recommendations, but consider a smart surge protector like this Tapo model ($42) to make a bigger difference.

These smart power strips let you name each included plug and port based on what you plug into them, and control them remotely, including through common apps like Google Home or Apple Home. You can also turn them on or off with voice commands when they are properly labeled in the app, which is neat if you have connected lights (more on that later) or fans.

Tapo’s version even allows you to track energy costs, which is a huge plus if you’re worried your desk equipment is sapping too much power.



A smart speaker for music and voice commands

Google’s new speaker does a lot right, especially when it comes to audio. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Yes, I like using my smart speaker for basic things like asking it about the weather and traffic, or setting a timer to remember to get up and stretch. But smart speakers can really put the “assistant” in voice assistant when you use them at a desk.

I cover this in more detail in guides like tricks for using Google Home and Nest, but you can use smart speakers to set reminders, add events to your calendar while you’re responding to an email or create a to-do list. Many also have other abilities that make them ready to help out. And they can connect to your streaming services to play music whenever you like.

These desk-friendly speakers are small but have very good audio for their size. Versions like the Echo Dot 5 are small and around $50, but for a big sound upgrade, consider something like the Echo Dot Max, Apple HomePod Mini or Google’s new Home Speaker.

That’s without getting into all the AI features of upgraded voice assistants like Gemini for Home or Alexa Plus. Alexa Plus is especially notable here because it’s free with an Amazon Prime subscription, and you can connect it with third-party services like Uber/Uber Eats, Ticketmaster, TaskRabbit and more for quick ordering while making plans.

A smart display for multitasking and dual-screen use

A Google control hub is great, especially when you get creative. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Think of a smart display as a smart speaker with a touchscreen. That can be surprisingly helpful, especially as a desktop companion. You get all the advantages of a smart speaker, plus the ability to check its work when it’s creating events or to-do lists — plus the option of watching videos, doing a quick internet search or even glancing through your video doorbell.

This second screen at the side of your computer can serve many in-depth purposes, too. You can get caught up in a show, view how-to videos or consult a gaming walkthrough while you’re playing. I’ve found smart displays a bit slower to react than tablets, but the sound is far better, so these displays are much easier to use as a music source or possibly a video chat.

Check out options like the Echo Show 11 ($220) and Nest Hub Max to see what I’m talking about.

Best Desktop Computer for 2026: Top Picks for Macs and PCs See at CNET

A smart heater for programmable, cost-saving heat

Radiant speakers are especially useful near home desks and offices. Boldr

Normal heaters are nice to have near your desk, but they can be fire hazards, energy hogs and aren’t always easy to operate. I suggest a smart upgrade. This radiant heater from Boldr ($400) is a high-end example, but you can see how it uses less electricity, poses fewer fire hazards and can be mounted on the wall to fit right by a desk without needing much space.

Also, don’t discount the ability to control a space heater via app. That allows you to set schedules to ensure your desk area is warm before you get there, or make sure the heater is turned off no matter where you are.

A smart lamp to set the mood and send reminders

Ikea’s lamp is smart, stylish and feels at home. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Lamps fit well on a computer desk, especially if you don’t have nearby lights or windows and need extra illumination. But a smart light version, like those in my guide, offers greater versatility and utility.

You can set a smart light to any brightness and color you want, letting you adjust the color temperature and make the light as easy on your eyes as you want. You can even connect these lights to other smart devices in the house to serve as visual notifications.

For example, you program the light to turn blue when a smart lock is unlocked, green when a door sensor is activated or red when a TV is turned on in another room.

You have a couple of options to adopt these smart lights. Depending on the size of the bulb, you may be able to upgrade an existing desk lamp with a smart bulb without changing anything else. Or you could replace a light with something like Ikea’s Varmblixt smart lamp if you have the room.

Light strips for fun and entertainment

For extra flair, today’s powerful lighting strips and panels offer many creative options. Govee

If you use your desk more for gaming, watching movies or other entertainment, consider a different kind of upgrade. Light strips set around the edges of your desk or monitor (or floor, etc.) can shift colors, flash along with music and match the theme of whatever you’re playing or watching. They typically need only one available outlet to get started and some can even be cut to size.

One of my favorite options for this is the Govee Gaming Light Rope, which lets you set scenes, sync to music and program it exactly how you want with the highly capable Govee app (which now includes an AI assistant you can give prompts to). In fact, you may want to take a look at Govee’s entire gaming and desk section, because there’s a lot there you can play with.

A nearby smart fan to help cool down

SwitchBot’s fan is a smart evolution for a bedroom or office fan, but not everyone needs so many features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

A large computer setup can grow hot, and there’s nothing like a fan to help cool things down, especially in summer heat waves. However, putting a fan directly on the desk takes up a lot of room and is too annoying for many people. I suggest putting fans at a distance in the same room instead. Our list of the best smart tower fans is an excellent place to get started. It’s surprisingly pleasant to be able to control your fan speed and direction at a distance with your phone (or smart display), but we have other, less complicated options, too.

If you have a nearby shelf or you prefer your fan up close and personal, you may also consider SwitchBot’s smart desk fan, which is the most advanced model I’ve ever tested.

Best Home Security Cameras of 2026: Smart Eyes Where You Need Them See at CNET

For more information, check out my guide on my favorite smart home devices in general, and the best tech for my home, even after my reviews were done.

Tech.title: The New Apple Watch Series 12 Is Almost Here, and It May Not Come Alone
Tech.content:
The Apple Watch may bring TouchID to the wrist. Vanessa Hand Orellana/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The Apple Watch is due for an upgrade, and if the company continues its tradition of September launches, we should be getting two new watches in the coming weeks. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing both an Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 for this fall, with faster chips and new health and fitness features, but no major design overhaul. Other wild-card rumors point to the return of a few throwback features, including a ceramic case, while leaked Apple code has fueled speculation that a fingerprint sensor (Touch ID) could finally make its way to the wrist.

As always, nothing is confirmed until Apple says so, but here’s everything we know, think we know and are crossing our fingers for.

Apple Watch Series 12 launch date

If there’s one thing Apple tends to keep consistent, it’s the timing of its fall hardware event, where it typically unveils its newest flagship iPhones and Apple Watch models.

Apple typically holds this event on the second Tuesday of September (usually the week after Labor Day). By that logic, Sept. 15 seems like the most likely candidate for Apple’s 2026 fall event. Because it lands a bit later in the month than in previous years, there’s also a chance Apple moves it up to Wednesday Sept. 9 (Labor Day week), as it has before.

As in previous years, preorders would typically open on the Friday after the event, with availability following a week or so later (assuming no production delays).

Pricing and availability

There are no solid rumors yet suggesting Apple will raise the price of its flagship Apple Watch, but the familiar $400 starting price (for the 42mm Wi-Fi model) isn’t guaranteed. Apple has raised prices across its hardware lineup this year, and Gurman expects some of this fall’s iPhones to get pricier too. Google and Samsung already raised prices on their 2026 flagship smartwatches, so a more expensive Apple Watch might not be out of the question.

The Apple Watch Ultra 3, SE 3 and Series 11 on launch day. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

How many Apple Watch models will we get?

A Series 12 is all but guaranteed — we’ve had a new Apple Watch model arrive every year since its launch. What’s less certain is whether Apple will refresh the entire lineup again this year. The Apple Watch SE and Ultra models don’t follow the same annual update cycle, and because both the SE 3 and Ultra 3 were refreshed in 2025, it’s unlikely Apple will update both again this year.

But since Apple isn’t one to gatekeep new features, and the Ultra 3 is still rocking a two-year-old chip at this point, it’s looking increasingly likely that it’ll get the same processor bump rumored for the Series 12, while keeping last year’s design. According to Gurman, Apple is preparing an Apple Watch Ultra 4 alongside the Series 12 for this fall, with both watches in late-stage testing.

Familiar design on the Apple Watch Series 12

Don’t hold your breath for a circular Apple Watch, or a major makeover (at least not for this year). Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said during a live Q&A on March 26 that no major design changes are expected for this year’s Apple Watch lineup, according to MacRumors. That aligns with how sparse the redesign chatter has been overall, so expect the same silhouette with similar colors and materials for both Apple Watch models.

What could change: screen technology. A more energy-efficient display — potentially an improved LTPO panel with better brightness, as seen on the Series 10 — could help claw back some battery life without adding bulk.

Better battery life tops the Apple Watch wish list year after year. Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

Battery life and processor

The Series 11 and Ultra 3 got a significant battery bump over their predecessors: at least 6 hours more by Apple’s numbers and roughly an extra half day (or more) in my real-world testing. And the Ultra 3 also got charging speed worthy of its name, like its newer siblings. But there’s still plenty of room for improvement on both battery life and charging speed.

This year, Apple may be going even bigger — literally. A Weibo leaker with a track record for Apple rumors says the company is prioritizing battery life on the Series 12, including a physically larger battery along with efficiency improvements elsewhere in the watch. If true, that could push battery life beyond the incremental gains we’ve seen in recent generations.

A new processor could help on the efficiency front too, and the Apple Watch is long overdue for one. All three 2025 Apple Watches are still running on the S10 chip, making an upgrade this year almost a given, especially with the new Siri AI arriving on the watch with WatchOS 27. Technically, the next processor in line would be the S11, but Apple usually matches the chip number to the flagship watch, which could mean skipping straight to the S12 this year.

New health features on the horizon

Apple has already dipped its toes into blood pressure monitoring with hypertension notifications on the Apple Watch (Series 10, Series 11 and Ultra 3). The feature alerts owners when it detects signs of abnormally high blood pressure, but it stops short of providing an on-the-spot read. This could be on the table for the fall of 2026.

Other wearable health companies like Omron and Med-Watch have proven that wrist-based blood pressure measurement is possible, though it’s not as reliable as a traditional cuff and may require new (bulkier) hardware to bring to the Apple Watch.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has been testing the feature internally but has encountered accuracy issues. And even if Apple pulls it off for this year, it might measure only baseline trends similar to Samsung’s blood pressure feature on the Galaxy Watch 7 and Ultra (not supported in the US).

Glucose monitoring is another long-running rumor that’s on the table, but according to Gurman, it’s even further from a finished product than blood pressure and realistically wouldn’t appear before 2027.

The next Apple Watch Series 12 may bring back TouchID. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Biometric authentication: Touch ID or Face ID?

Rumors of a camera on the Apple Watch have been around for a few years — not for selfies, but potentially for Face ID or AI-based image recognition.

Apple Intelligence on the iPhone introduced a visual search tool that uses the camera to identify objects and places in real time, and it might be a matter of time before this feature eventually makes its way to the wrist. Meanwhile, wearable-focused processors like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips already support cameras and even livestreaming. Apple is known for using its proprietary chips, so it’s unlikely this would affect its timeline, but it shows the technology is there, and we may see it on the Apple Watch down the line. Just not this year, according to Bloomberg.

A more feasible near-term option could be Touch ID. Macworld recently spotted lines of internal code suggesting Apple has been experimenting with biometric authentication for either the 2026 or 2027 Apple Watch lineup. According to the report, the code references “AppleMesa,” which is Apple’s internal code name for a watch-based Touch ID. It’s still unclear whether the sensor would be integrated under the display, like we see on Android phones, or built into the side button or the Digital Crown.

A supercharged Watch OS 27

We already know the next batch of Apple Watches will ship with WatchOS 27, and I’ve already been testing it out in beta. The biggest upgrade by far is Siri AI, which can answer more complex questions directly on your wrist instead of defaulting to the dreaded “Here’s what I found on the web.”

In my testing, Siri AI successfully answered questions about ferry schedules, recipes and World Cup matches that old Siri either couldn’t answer completely or kicked over to web results. It’s the first time I’ve intentionally wanted to use Siri on my Apple Watch, and it could be an even bigger reason to upgrade than any of the rumored hardware changes, especially because it’s not that snappy on my Series 11 (could still be the beta) and could benefit from that extra processing power.

WatchOS 27 also brings a smarter app grid and Smart Stack, expanded one-handed gesture controls, improved workout accuracy and new perimenopause insights. While Apple’s pseudo AI coach, Workout Buddy will be available in Spanish and can finally work without an iPhone nearby, though it’s still more motivational hype companion than full-fledged AI coach.

The catch is that WatchOS 27 leaves a lot of older watches behind: You’ll need a Series 9 or newer, Ultra 2 or newer or the SE 3 to get the update. That makes this year’s software upgrade particularly relevant if you’re hanging onto an older Apple Watch.

A future Apple Watch could bring advanced health sensors for on-the-spot blood pressure reads. Tharon Green / CNET

Health app updates beyond WatchOS 27

Though not coming with the initial WatchOS 27 update, Apple has also been rumored to be prepping a major overhaul of its Health app. According to a report from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, Apple has been working on a top-secret initiative code-named Project Mulberry, aimed at revamping the Health app with an AI-powered health concierge that could unify your health, fitness, and medical data in one place.

However, the project has recently run into some obstacles. Bloomberg’s latest report suggests Apple has put the effort on hold (at least for this year). That still leaves room for improvement on the Health app front with a potential redesign to the main dashboard that would make spotting trends easier.

Of course, even the most credible rumors are still just rumors, and we won’t know anything for certain until Apple’s official launch event. We’ll be covering all the announcements as they happen, so check back for the latest updates.

Tech.title: iOS 27 Is Almost Here, but You Should Check Out All These iOS 26 Features First
Tech.content:
Apple/CNET

Apple announced iOS 27 and more at its 2026 Worldwide Developers Conference in June. The upcoming iPhone operating system will introduce Siri AI and a handful of other features to compatible devices this fall. Based on historical trends, Apple could release iOS 27 to the general public in mid-September. Before then, now is a good time to check out all the features iOS 26 and its updates brought to your device over the past year.

Apple released that update in September 2025, and it introduced call screening and other features to your device. The update also gave your iPhone Liquid Glass, the first major design shift on the device since Apple released iOS 7 in 2013.

Tech.title: Americans Want to Know When Their Healthcare Providers Use AI
Tech.content:
AI chatbots are being used in healthcare, both in and out of the doctor’s office, more than ever before. Patient and medical providers alike are turning to AI for treatments and diagnoses, but transparency remains a key concern, a new survey by Pew Research Center shows.

A poll of 3,488 US adults conducted between June 22 and June 28 found that a quarter of respondents use chatbots to diagnose symptoms. Those turning to chatbots for health mainly cite convenience and affordability as their motive. Patients also use AI chatbots to find information quickly and at no cost, better understand a doctor’s diagnosis, interpret lab results and decide whether to seek in-person care.

Of these survey participants, almost half (47%) say the health information generated by the chatbot was “extremely” helpful, and 48% said the information was “somewhat” helpful. Only 5% said the results were not too helpful or not at all helpful.

AI chatbots work by simulating a conversation between two parties and responding to your prompts or inputs using the massive amounts of information the models were trained on. Many people appreciate the convenience they offer, as chatbots are available 24/7 and can often be accessed for free and sometimes without an account. Chatbots, however, are known to “hallucinate,” or generate false information in their responses, which can be particularly dangerous or alarming when your personal health is in question. Among other issues, they’re trained to produce a probable answer, not necessarily one grounded in truth, and they’re likely to sound particularly confident about that answer.

But generative artificial intelligence is also showing up at the doctor’s office — and Pew found that Americans have greater concerns about its use there.

Read also: ChatGPT Health Will See You Now, and It’s a Big Step Forward for Medical Queries

When doctors turn to chatbots

While recent numbers show that about one in three US adults have used chatbots for health-related questions, medical providers are also increasingly turning to AI in the office for note-taking, interpreting exams and more.

While views on AI use in doctors’ offices vary, one factor remains of critical concern to patients: transparency.

Of those surveyed, 72% say it is “extremely or very important” for their medical provider to disclose any use of AI. The survey also found that a vast majority of people (eight in 10) want to be told if AI is being used directly for care or medical decisions, such as diagnoses and the analysis of scans, X-rays and lab results. AI is frequently used for triage purposes — and has even been shown to outperform human ER doctors — as well as to complete clinical tasks more quickly. For instance, AI has been used effectively to reduce the window of X-ray interpretations from 11.2 to 2.7 days.

Although Americans want advance notice when AI is used in their healthcare, nearly half (47%) are unsure whether it has ever played a role in their treatment, underscoring limited awareness of when, where and how the technology is used.

Americans are not fully comfortable with AI

The survey shows that Americans may find AI chatbots convenient, but not entirely trustworthy.

Views are mixed on sharing personal health histories and diagnoses with AI. Among those surveyed, 29% say they are extremely or very comfortable sharing health information with chatbots, while 26% say they are uncomfortable doing so.

The findings suggest that although AI is increasingly used for health information and care, public confidence and understanding have not kept pace with its adoption.

Tech.title: Behind the Scenes of ESPN’s Animated Sports Alt-Casts
Tech.content:
When ESPN floated the idea of creating an animated alternative broadcast for games, it was all about creating “magical moments in sports.” Instead of watching sports stars shooting hoops or scoring touchdowns, there was suddenly an option to see Mickey Mouse, Buzz Lightyear, Lisa Simpson or Mike Wazowski do the honors.

For Michael “Spike” Szykowny, ESPN vice president of edit, animation, graphics innovation and creative production, this project is his baby. The animated alt-casts bring a different audience to sports, Szykowny said during a panel at Disney’s D23 convention last weekend.

“We took a bunch of technologies like live player tracking — we can track what the players are doing in the game and make our animated characters do the same things,” Szykowny said. ESPN brought Disney IP into the project and combined it with face-tracking and motion-capture technology.

ESPN studio host Drew Carter has been a live animated commentator for every alt-cast. He said that for the first one, he had to wear a full motion-capture suit. But now, he only has to wear a virtual reality headset.

“It’s a technological feat to track these players in real time,” Jay Ward, creative director of franchise at Pixar, said during the panel in Anaheim, California.

The players on the field wear devices that generate tracking data for NFL Next Gen Stats and into Sony’s Beyond Sports engine and Sony’s Hawk-Eye Innovations optical tracking. These technologies are then used to create live animations, “rebuilding each throw, route, block, kick and tackle in real time,” Disney says.

The commentators’ booth calls are synced with their animated avatars via their VR headsets.

Ward said Pixar wanted to be involved because the animation studio “is all about technology, creativity and storytelling.”

During the Toy Story version of Funday Football, which aired in 2023, the main toys were all seen playing an NFL game in Andy’s room, with the real players as toy-scale versions of themselves.

Blocks were used for goalposts; the claw machine manned by the three-eyed aliens brought the ball down for kickoff; Slinky Dog was the 1st and 10 marker; and there was a Duke Caboom halftime show. Carter appeared as a Pixar-ified version of himself doing the commentary on-screen.

The second iteration of Funday Football featured the characters of Monsters, Inc., and the scene had to be animated from scratch because the movie is 25 years old.

Random players were picked to become Mike and Sulley playing on the field, while the other players were just animated versions of themselves, and Roz was a sideline reporter. All the original voice actors from the Pixar movie returned to help with the alt-cast, as did Carter.

Dunk the Halls, a Christmas NBA game played between Mickey and his closest friends in December last year, was next. It was animated to look as if it were being played on a perfect replica of Main Street, USA, at Walt Disney World, with the team even bringing in animators from Walt Disney Studios to get it right.

Disney Legend and iconic animator Eric Goldberg drew hundreds of sketches of what “bits” the characters could do during the game.

But there was a problem.

“The tracking was off at one point,” said Renée Johnson, creative director of Disney Character Voices. The referee was accidentally turned into a player who scored a 3-pointer, so they quickly turned the character into Stitch.

ESPN tried its hand at an NHL game next, choosing the Pixar film Inside Out, given that the main character plays hockey. The game was designed to look like it’s being played inside Riley’s mind while she’s sleeping, with the ESPN Beyond Sports animation team building out Hockey Island in three dimensions for the alt-cast setting. That game aired in March this year and used NHL positional data for the players and puck, along with Sony Hawk-Eye Innovations’ optical tracking.

And for a Simpsons-themed Funday Football session in December 2024, ESPN brought in the whole Simpsons writing team.

“There was a little bit of fear because these are three giant iconic brands: NFL, The Simpsons and Disney — how will they work together?” said Joel Cohen, a writer and co-executive producer of The Simpsons. “We’re very particular about how we want our characters to be portrayed and what jokes we want them to tell.”

The team came up with 8 minutes of original Simpsons animation with a storyline that carried throughout the game. Animating for a live event is something that the animation team never gets to do, so it was “a super fun vibe that we never get to experience,” Cohen said, adding that even creator Matt Groening came along.

The writers of The Simpsons were texting Disney and ESPN during the event — though the NFL said no to some of the jokes the writers came up with.

“There’s a 1-minute delay, so we can see what play happens to insert characters and push forward the storyline,” Szykowny said. “(Like) quickly put Bart as QB, Lisa as receiver as they score.”

ESPN has yet to announce its next animated alt-cast, but the animation x sports project isn’t showing any signs of slowing down. You can rewatch the alt-casts on YouTube, Disney Plus and ESPN Plus, but they’re much more impressive to witness live, simultaneously with a game.

Tech.title: A New Interactive Tool Weighs Vaccine Risks for You
Tech.content:
We live in a time when mixed messages about vaccines are the norm. Often, the Trump administration says one thing, while public health officials say another, leaving at least half of Americans in what the independent health policy organization KFF called the “malleable middle.” They remain uncertain when presented with vaccine myths.

To address the confusion, the free “What’s the Risk?” tool launched in early August. It allows users to visualize the vaccine risks often described as “rare” or “uncommon” right alongside the risks associated with the diseases they were created to prevent.

The interactive tool was designed by the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy and Unbiased Science, a public health communication platform and podcast founded by Jessica Steier, a public health scientist.

More comparisons will be added over time, but right now, you can see the measles and the MMR vaccine and RSV alongside its vaccines and antibody products. Plus, you can compare them to life events, such as deaths caused by drowning, car crashes, falls, bee or wasp stings and lightning strikes.

How to use the vaccine risk tool

First, choose one of the suggested comparisons or build your own by selecting two from the dropdowns.

Life events like drowning and car crashes help put certain risks in perspective. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

But before you scroll down to see the comparison, Steier told CNET in an email that you should read the “Before you compare: a few things to know” list at the top. It explains, for example, that what happens if you get infected versus what happens if you get vaccinated aren’t equally likely. For the former, it depends on many factors, such as where you live and travel and how many people around you are vaccinated.

“They tell you what each side of the comparison is holding constant, and that shapes how you should read everything below it,” Steier said.

Scroll down to view the two side-by-side light gray boxes. Each represents 100,000 people in the population indicated above the boxes in color-coded bands. Comparisons are most reliable when comparing the same population, so when two different age groups are shown, you should treat the results as a rough sense of scale rather than a precise number.

Sources are shown below the squares, along with each risk and the number of those affected per 100,000 of the stated population. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Plus, these are population averages. Your personal risk will depend on your age, health status and lifestyle circumstances.

All numbers are shown as an annual rate, unless labeled otherwise. Since everyday risks are usually published as lifetime figures, those had to be converted.

Within the light gray boxes, you’ll find colored squares representing each risk. They’re sized to indicate the number of people affected by the stated complication. “A very rare outcome shows up as a tiny speck and a common one as a large block,” said Steier.

Each square has a color meant to illustrate the severity of the outcome. Red indicates serious outcomes, while dark gray indicates those considered mild or temporary.

If you hover over a square or tap on it, you can read the details and see links to the sources for the number shown by the square.

Above the squares, you can switch to a grid view for a different perspective. You can also zoom in to see the risks represented in a population of 50,000.

What the grid view looks like. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Ultimately, this tool takes numbers that can be difficult to contextualize and helps you visualize them to better understand the relative frequency and severity of vaccines versus their connected diseases.

How sources were chosen

To narrow down the sources for this tool, two rules were applied. “Every figure has to come from a public, citable source, and every figure has to be measured the same way as the one sitting next to it,” said Steier.

For the first rule, the tool’s creators went straight to the source: national surveillance systems and published studies, rather than news articles, fact sheets or advocacy pages that merely cited the original data. The tool links out to these sources, in case you’d like to check their work.

When you hover over a risk, you can see the sources used. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The makers also matched both the vaccine and disease sides based on age group and population as closely as available data allowed. Where that match isn’t exact, the tool says so.

The goal

A single number or statistic won’t typically tell you everything you need to know when it comes to vaccine or disease risk. According to Steier, to understand a risk, you need three things: how likely the outcome is, how serious it would be if it happened, and what it compares to, including what happens if you do nothing.

“Part of what we’re up against is numbness,” said Steier. “Everyone throws scary numbers around constantly, so we’ve stopped registering them. ‘One in 10,000’ and ‘one in a million’ both just land as ‘rare,’ even though one is a hundred times the other.”

The hope with this tool is that users will better understand what those numbers actually mean and develop a habit of asking “compared to what?”

While not directly comparable due to age differences, it’s still eye-opening to compare vaccine complications with life events. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The tool’s future

In addition to working on the design and functionality, the team behind “What’s the Risk?” plans to add more vaccines and diseases. Plus, everyday life events, since those help people put an unfamiliar risk on a scale they already understand.

“The addition we’re most excited about is a way to reflect vaccine coverage, because coverage is what drives how likely you are to encounter these diseases in the first place,” Steier said. This could involve pulling in vaccine uptake by ZIP code so people can view their community, or a slider that lets users adjust vaccine coverage to see how disease risk changes.

This expansion would show that many of us live with a low risk of disease because of the number of people around us who are vaccinated.

Steier emphasized that the current version of the tool is merely version 1.0, so if you see anything that can be improved, you can email the team at vaccines@unbiasedscience.com.

Tech.title: Percy Jackson Cast Teases ‘Some People Get What They Deserve’ in Season 3
Tech.content:
The third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians is fast approaching, and at Disney’s D23 convention in Anaheim, California, last weekend, we got a glimpse of what’s to come as the cast answered fan questions during a panel discussion.

Earlier during Disney’s D23 Entertainment Showcase, the show got a fresh, new trailer for November’s third season. Walker Scobell, who plays the title character of Percy Jackson, was joined on stage by Ming-Na Wen (Hera) and Andra Day (Athena) to present the new trailer, which showed Percy fighting underwater and in arenas as a titan emerges.

After the ill-fated, critically panned movies released in the 2010s made it only to the second book in Rick Riordan’s series, the Disney Plus original will be the first time The Titan’s Curse has gotten an adaptation. It follows Percy and his Camp Half-Blood crew on their mission to rescue the goddess Artemis (played by Dafne Keen).

“Season 3 is the season where some people get what they deserve,” Scobell said during Saturday’s panel. There will also be a lot of improv in season 3, Scobell said, with the cast now close enough to play off each other like siblings bantering (which they did, all panel long, arguing over who is the most powerful).

Tamara Smart, who plays Thalia, said scenes exploring the past and Olympus were her favorites to shoot. “Season 3 is the season where women run it,” she said.

“It’s great to play a powerful, confident woman,” Smart added. “She’s 100% angry, 100% sad, 100% yelling at Percy.” (She added that after every single take where she was forced to yell at Scobell, she apologized to him.)

Keen wasn’t allowed to tease much from the upcoming season, but said the newcomers to the show had a huntress camp where they all got to train together, learn as a pack and master archery.

“Love and loss inform all decisions,” she said of Season 3.

Saara Chaudry said bringing Zoë Nightshade to life in the new season “has been the absolute privilege of my life.”

“Season 3 is the season where the stars align,” Chaudry added.

Dan Shotz, a showrunner, writer and executive producer, had some more detailed hints about the upcoming season.

“We have this great source material, and we get to dive a lot deeper… You’re going to see all these great things you love from this book, but so much more,” he said. “We cannot have a season of this show without Annabeth.”

Shotz said we will meet all the gods this season, as well as get to see the junkyard of the gods.

But not everyone makes it out alive, executive producer Jonathan Steinberg said.

“I’m excited for everyone to go on that ride shown in the trailer,” Steinberg said. “The trailer doesn’t lie.”

The eight-episode season streams on Nov. 20 on Disney Plus.
